The CHAPTER XLV. 

PLEADINGS. 

290. PETITIONS. 

Aside from accounting and its incidents, the major portion of the jurisdiction of the orphans' court is invoked by petition. The specific purposes for which such relief is applicable are herein discussed under the particular subjects involved. 

Under the broad equitable doctrines and principles through which the orphans' court administers justice almost any desired relief may be obtained by this flexible method of procedure. 33 The essential features of all petitions are as follows: 

1. The formal caption and heading indicating briefly the object. 

2. A recital of the facts giving the court jurisdiction of the subject matter. 

3. A recital of all parties interested" in the estate or the subject matter of the petition, with their status as to minority, etc., and a statement as to notice by joinder or otherwise. 

4. A recital where necessary of the impelling motive for presenting the petition and the reasons why the relief prayed for is of advantage to the estate. 

5. The prayer for the desired relief, drafted with exactness so that the decree can as far as possible follow it verbatim. 

6. Signature and affidavit of petitioner. 

7. Formal joinder of all parties where possible. 

33 "No immaterial variation from the forms given and prescribed in and by this act, shall vitiate or render void any proceedings in which said forms shall be used." Fiduciaries Act of 1917 (P. L. 447), Sec. 61, which is 

Section 43 of the Act of March 15, 1832, (P. L. 135), 1 Purd. 1072. See also Purd. Stat. Ann. Tit. 20, Sec. 1141.

The court has complete control of proceedings arising on petition and can allow an amendment thereof upon terms. Deagler's Est., 14 D. & C. 598. 

34 Where partition proceedings have been instituted in the orphans' court, but one of the parties has been inadvertently omitted from the petition, such omission may be corrected by amendment. Doyle's Est., 291 Pa. 263. 757

§§ 290, 291 

8. Exhibits, always including a complete copy of the will or deed of trust where an instrument is involved. 

9. The decree carefully drawn to cover exactly the relief sought and following as closely as possible the language of the prayer.35

All recitals of fact should be exact, especially as to names, dates and descriptions of real estate. This will frequently save the embarrassing necessity of later presenting a petition to amend." 36 Where such a course is necessary the petition should recite the former proceedings, quote exactly the decree then entered, outline the desired amendment, join all parties in interest and annex a new decree specifically amending the former decree as desired. 

291. ANSWERS. 

Where all parties in interest for any reason do not join in the petition or where it is adverse the prayer should be for a citations directed to the respondents, or parties 35 By a ruling of the orphans' court of Philadelphia County the decree must be placed before the body of the petition and form the first page thereof. 

36 A petition may be amended, when the defect is merely in form: 

Chess's App., 4 Pa. 52; Downer v. Downer, 9 Pa. 302; Pote's App., 106 Pa. 574; Hay's Est., 33 P. L. J. 414; Stewart's Est., 7 Pa. C. C. 

603, 20 Phila. 9, 47 L. I. 49. And may be treated as amended, both in the court below, and in the appellate courts: Knecht's App., 71 Pa. 333; 

Wilson's App., 3 Walk. 216; Young's Est., 14 Pa. C. C. 547, 3 Dist. 282, 34 W. N. C. 165. The petition may be amended, even after answer filed, if notice is given to the respondent, or he has waived the right to answer further: Greble's Est., 9 Dist. 441. But when the petitioner sues in the wrong capacity, and thereby puts himself beyond the jurisdiction of the court, the defect cannot be remedied by rendering a decree in his favor in another capacity: Olwine's App., 4 W. & S. 492. And an amendment will not be allowed, when the parties have been guilty of great laches: 

Stewart's App., 19 P. L. J. 73.

A petition which is indefinite and uncertain will be dismissed: Davis's 

Est., 6 W. N. C. 15, 12 Phila. 128, 35 L. I. 274. Graham's Est., 14 W. N. C. 31.

To such petition the respondents may of course file an answer where it is desired to raise a question of law or fact, though technically the former might better be termed a demurrer.38 

Such answer should be under oath; should admit paragraph by paragraph all matters of fact admittedly correct, and with equal clearness deny such averments as are claimed to be incorrect with sufficient exactness where possible to show the basis for the denial.38a 

There may also be included in the answer any counteraverments of fact deemed pertinent to the issue. 

Needless to say the answer should in every case be signed and sworn to by the respondents.

Separate answers may be filed by each respondent if desired or any number may join in the same pleading. 

If the answer" raise an issue of law alone, the matter is heard at the argument list on petition and answer. If an issue of fact be raised it is tried by the court or a master after replication filed.39a

The proceedings in the orphans' court should be in form substantially as in equity, i. e., by petition, answer and replication, but technical precision is not required: Steffy's App., 76 Pa. 94; Markle's Est., 16 Pa. C. C. 

397, 4 Dist. 348; Worthington's Est., 6 Super. 484, affirming 9 Kulp, 129, 16 Lanc. 46. The equity rules of the supreme court are part of the rules of the orphans' court: Stoker's Est., 25 Pa. C. C. 619, 10 Dist. 375.

The answer must be fully responsive to the petition: Davis's Est., 9

 292. DEMURRERS. 

Such pleadings are of rather infrequent use but are apt¹º where it is desired to raise a point of law going directly to the legal sufficiency of the prior pleading without a hearing on the merits or issue of fact, if any." 42 Such demurrers 12 need not be under oath and are customarily filed by counsel for the demurrant raising successively the points of law to which objection is made" followed in each case with the reasons applicable thereto. 43 If the point of law is so apparent that argument would be useless, a decree may be entered at once, otherwise the matter should appear on the next argument list of the court.

Under the equity rules in lieu of a demurrer the practice has developed in certain jurisdictions of filing pre- 

40 Darrach's Est., 2 Clark 454; Montgomery's Est., 3 Brewst. 306.

It is not proper practice for one petitioning for a citation by the orphans' court to file an argumentative demurrer to respondent's answer; the case must be determined on petition and answer. Olanoff's Est., 21 D. & C. 652. 

41 A demurrer and answer cannot stand together, and a subsequent answer overrules a demurrer unless it be withdrawn by leave of court: 

Montgomery's Est., 3 Brewst. 306; Cram's Est., 25 W. N. C. 250; Finley's

When the answer to a petition is insufficient, the proper practice is to demur; exceptions are not equivalent to a demurrer or replication, and cannot form the basis of a judgment. If, however, exceptions have been filed, the court will grant leave, in a proper case, to file a replication and take testimony: Reichner's 

Est., 32 Pa. C. C. 498, 14 Dist. 789. The petitioner may discontinue on payment of costs; and the respondent's counsel fees are not included in the costs: Hanbest's Est., 3 W. N. C. 28; Harrah's Est., 7 Dist. 698.

On a demurrer to a petition in the orphans' court, raising the question of the jurisdiction of the court, the averments in the petition must be taken as true. Greenaway's Est., 38 York 169.

An averment in a petition by trustees of a church which is being abandoned that, as the result of a merger, the organization to which it asks leave to turn over certain trust funds is the same entity as a previously existing body, is an averment of fact rather than a legal conclusion, and is therefore admitted by a demurrer to the petition. Minuteness and specification is required in all legal proceedings. It should be stated wherein the writ is uncertain, informal and insufficient. We have carefully examined the writ of citation and can find no defect in it. 

It was issued by the clerk of the orphans' court in the usual form, properly attested and properly served. We think it is correct." Potter, P. J., in

293. REPLICATIONS. 

Where an issue of fact is raised by the petition and answer, a replication" should be filed by the petitioner. 

Until this is done the matter cannot regularly proceed further. An argument on petition and answer without replication will be treated as an admission that the averments in the answer are true and correct.45 

The replication having been filed the issue raised will be heard by the court, where the exigencies of the case require it, or, more generally, by a master appointed for the purpose. 46 44 The office of the replication is to put the respondent to proof of the allegations in the answer set up by way of confession and avoidance: 

Sterr's Est., 7 W. N. C. 35, 13 Phila. 212, 36 L. I. 137. The replication must be general; a special replication is forbidden by the equity rules; and new matter set up in the replication must be brought into the petition by amendment: Morrow's Est., 15 W. N. C. 240, 16 Phila. 387, 41 L. I. 

428; Stoker's Est., 25 Pa. C. C. 619, 10 Dist. 375. But if the parties acquiesce in the pleadings, and go on to final decree, the respondent cannot then set up the irregularity in filing a special replication without amending the petition: Miller's Est., 174 Pa. 362.

A special replication averring new matter is forbidden by the Equity Rules; the proper practice is to amend the petition by leave of court. 

Troelsch's Est., 17 Dist. 518. 

See Form No. 251, App., p. 292. 

45 Good's Est., 35 Super. 440. And in the absence of proofs, the answer will be taken to be true though replication has been filed: Wilt's 

Est., 13 Dist. 483; Sterr's Est., 7 W. N. C. 35, 13 Phila. 212, 36 L. I. 137.

The equity rule which requires the evidence of two witnesses, or of one witness and corroborating circumstances, to overcome a sworn answer, is applied in the orphans' court: Krogman's Est., 14 Pa. C. C. 567, 34 W.

N. C. 104. And the answer is to be taken as true, if not denied or disproved: Long's Est., 168 Pa. 341; Oberley's Est., 5 North. 337. When the case is set down for hearing on petition and answer, all the averments of the answer are to be taken as true: Russell's Administrator's App., 34 Pa. 258; Kellberg's App., 86 Pa. 129, reversing 4 W. N. C. 478; Conrad's Est., 13 Phila. 207, 36 L. I. 84; Mercur's Est., 151 Pa. 49; Souder's 

Est. (No. 2), 169 Pa. 239; Schmidt's Est., 16 Pa. C. C. 299, 4 Dist. 161, 36 W. N. C. 152; Wood's Est., 7 Dist. 655; Palethorp's Est., 7 Dist. 699.

And the same is true when the case is set down for hearing on petition, answer and replication, without giving the respondent an opportunity of taking evidence in support of his answer: Sterr's Est., 7 W. N. C. 35, 13 Phila. 212, 36 L. I. 137; Cremer's Est., 7 W. N. C. 544, 13 Phila. 253, 36 L I. 286; Berryman's Est., 16 W. N. C. 303, 17 Phila. 463, 42 L. I.

§§ 294, 295  294. EXCEPTIONS. 

Closely akin to the right to answer is the right to file exceptions. The former is generally limited to proceedings begun by petition to show cause. The latter is almost entirely governed by rule of court. Only in the case of exceptions to bonds taken by the register is the right specifically recognized by statute" and by inference in the matter of accounting.48

By the rules of the orphans' court exceptions may be filed to auditors' reports," masters' reports,5° accounts,51 adjudications,52 petitions for the widow's exemption 53 or allowance, schedules of distribution,55 etc. The form, method of filing 56 and disposition of such exceptions have been considered under the specific subjects involved. 

If for any reason the exceptions appear to have been improperly taken and it is impracticable to await their disposition at the next argument list there may be filed a petition" to show cause why the exceptions should not be stricken off.

The most important duty is that of promptly and efficiently filing with the court making the appointment a report of their findings of fact" and law and in the case of masters and auditors their recommendations thereon either in the form of a proposed decree or otherwise. 

To such reports any party in interest may except if such exceptions have not been waived, and it is the duty of the master or auditor to pass upon such exceptions concurrently with the filing of his final report. 

296. MISCELLANEOUS PLEAS, ORDERS AND MOTIONS. 

Motions, other than those for the appointment of a master or auditor are preferably presented in the form of a petition to show cause. 

Orders are generally limited to matters pro forma, such as orders to the clerk ordering down cases on the motion, audit, or argument lists and are covered by rule of court. 

Stipulations may be filed covering agreements by counsel as to matters of fact or evidence or compromising claims, etc. Such should be in writing and in some jurisdictions this is mandatory.75 

The withdrawal of exceptions, etc., is also allowed as a part of the pleadings, though in certain instances an allocatur must be secured.75 

74 While it is the duty of a court in banc to review carefully all findings of fact by a master which have been made the subject of exceptions, such a finding will not be set aside except upon the discovery of some plain and obvious error or so great a preponderance of evidence against the finding that were it the verdict of a jury a new trial would be granted. Schmidt's 

Est., 18 D. & C. 567.

Finding of fact of the master, supported by competent evidence and approved by the lower court, will not on appeal be disturbed by the appellate court. Mathues's Est., 322 Pa. 358. 

74a Since the passage of the Act of July 1, 1937 (P. L. 2665), relating to juries drawn in the Orphans' Court (Sec. 314, n. 56a infra) Phila. County has provided by amendment to Rule 1, subsec. (I) that "motions for new trial, motions to take off non-suits, and for judgments n. o. v. and such other motions as may be made after jury trials shall be placed by the clerk, as of course, on the argument list.'' The form of these motions, except for obvious changes, as in the caption, etc., should be the same as those acceptable in the courts of common pleas of the various counties. 

75 In Phila. County and possibly others.

CHAPTER XLVI. 

PROCEDURE TO OBTAIN APPEARANCE. 

297. CITATION AND SERVICE. 

Persons amenable to its jurisdiction" may be cited by the orphans' court to appear or proceedings had on their default, as it is provided: "The manner of proceeding in the orphans' court, to obtain the appearance of a person" amenable to its jurisdiction, and the procedure in default of appearance, shall be as follows: 

"On petition" to the court of any person interested," 76 i. e. parties interested in the proceeding. The subpœnaing of witnesses is considered subsequently. See Sec. 307, infra.

The court cannot make an order on any person or corporation which is not a party to the record and not in court under proper order or process. 

Dench's Est., 14 Erie 93, 17 D. & C. 696. 

77 A person, after answering the averments of a petition for a citation, and, after appearing and taking testimony, cannot raise the question whether or not a citation, not directed to any person and no return day appearing therein, is sufficient. Stephens' Est., 10 Leh. 337. 

78 This act is imperative in directing the manner of proceeding in the orphans' court, to obtain the appearance of a person amenable to its jurisdiction, and to compel obedience to its orders and decrees: Okeson's 

App., 2 Gr. 303; Olwine's App., 4 W. & S. 492; Wooley's Est., 6 Pa. 

351; Johnson's App., 9 Pa. 416; Stewart's App., 19 P. L. J. 73; Davis's 

Est., 6 W. N. C. 15, 12 Phila. 128, 35 L. I. 274.

A citation will not issue upon a mere affidavit: Cramp's Est., 1 Camp. 

209, 3 Leg. Gaz. 203. Or upon a motion filed in the clerk's office: Ward's 

Est., 1 W. N. C. 418, 2 Luz. L. T. O. S. 143. Nor has the orphans' court jurisdiction of a case stated: Wilen's Est., 8 Phila. 210, 28 L. I. 117; 

Holt's Est., 1 W. N. C. 172, 11 Phila. 13, 32 L. I. 29; Sharpe's Est., 1 W. N. C. 405; but see Keene's App., 60 Pa. 504. 

79 This includes the partial assignee of a legacy: Thompson's App., 103 

Pa. 603. In proceedings to enforce the payment of legacies, all the legatees may join in one petition: Baker's App., 59 Pa. 313.

The petitioner must be a person interested: Olwine's App., 4 W. & 

S. 492; Halsey v. Tate, 52 Pa. 311. And the petition must show the interest of the party: Madden's Est., 6 Luz. L. Reg. 201, 8 Leg. Gaz. 95; 

Fry's Est., 7 Lanc. 107: Okeson's App., 2 Gr. 303. An agent cannot petition, though acting under a power of attorney: Madden's Est., 6 Luz. 

Leg. 201, 8 Leg. Gaz. 95. And a person of full age, though mentally incapacitated, cannot petition by next friend; he can act only by a committee: Kline's Est., 9 Dist. 386. If one who is not interested obtains a citation the proper practice is to deny his interest in the answer: Lightner's Est., 144 Pa. 273; Star's Est., 3 Super. 212.

But a mere creditor of the personal representative cannot do so: Gallagher's Est., 8 Dist. 699. Nor a judgment creditor of a legatee: Greiner's Est., 2 W. 

N. C. 292. Nor an attaching creditor of the share of a distributee payable in the discretion of a trustee: Locher's Est., 18 Lanc. Rev. 6.

One who is simply a surety for the administrator of an estate cannot be said to be interested in the estate of which his principal is the administrator, although the administrator fails to account for and pay the trust property and funds which came into his hands and thereby the surety becomes a debtor of the estate, and therefore under the above section such surety has no standing to require his principal, who is the administrator, to pay adjudicated claims. Seidman's Est., 20 Lack. 176, citing Moore's

CHAPTER XLVII. 

PROCEEDINGS TO ENFORCE ORDERS AND DECREES. 

300. METHODS OF PROCEDURE. 

Six methods of procedure are open to enforce compliance with an order" or decree of the orphans' court: 

1. Attachment of the person. 

100 99 The orphans' court has always had full and plenary authority to enforce compliance with its orders and decrees: Bowman v. Herr, 1 P. & W. 282; Black v. Black, 34 Pa. 354; Donaldson v. Miller, 23 Pa. C. C. 

393, s. c. sub. nom. Irwin's Est., 9 Dist. 282.

All known remedies at law and equity are given, and the orphans' court may afford relief by sequestration, attachment, and common law forms of execution: Tome's App., 50 Pa. 285; Ex parte Batdorf, 13 W. N. C. 

417, 2 Dauph. 287.

An attachment cannot issue against an executor to enforce the payment of a legacy until after a definite decree to pay a specific sum to a certain person has been made. Wilt's Est. (No. 2), 46 York 133. 

100 Orphans' Court Act of 1917 (P. L. 363), Sec. 18 (a), 1 based on Clause XI of Sec. 57 of the Act of March 29, 1832 (P. L. 190), 3 Purd. 

3375 (n-r) and repealing Sec. 8 of the Act of March 27, 1713, (1 Sm. L. 

81). (See ex parte Batdorf, 13 W. N. C. 417.) See Sec. 301, infra. See also Purd. Stat. Ann. Tit. 20, Sec. 2372-6; Weaver's Est., 114 Super. 439; 

Braunschweiger's Est., 322 Pa. 394.

The orphans' court has power to enforce, against the person of a dismissed executor, by process of attachment, a decree that he should pay and deliver over to his successor all the goods, chattels and effects of the estate in his hands: Tome's App., 50 Pa. 285. An attachment will issue to enforce payment of costs or fees imposed on the accountant personally: 

Lundy's Est., 3 C. P. Rep. 139; Hoffman's Est., 10 Super. 113; Patton's

Est., 19 Super. 545. But not to compel an insolvent executor to pay a personal debt to the testator: Royal's Est., 16 Phila. 249, 40 L. I. 171.

An attachment will be allowed only when the ordinary process is inadequate: Hofelt's Est., 45 P. L. J. 402. And when asked for to enforce payment of a distributive share, a fi. fa. will be first directed: Abrahim's 

Est., 3 Pa. C. C. 379, 19 W. N. C. 450. An attachment will be refused, when the accountant's failure to comply with the decree is due solely to his insolvency, existing prior to the accounting: Stevenson's Est., 7 

W. N. C. 65, 13 Phila. 209, 36 L. I. 105; Donaldson v. Miller, 23 Pa.

C. C. 393, s. c. sub. nom. Irwin's Est., 9 Dist. 282. Unless his inability to pay is due to his own misconduct: Leiter's App., 10 W. N. C. 225; Croop v. 

Freas, 8 Pa. C. C. 107. An attachment may issue, though a writ of sequestration has been partially executed: Tome's App., 50 Pa. 285. But not when a fi. fa. has been levied and is not yet disposed of: Kneedler's 

Est., 4 W. N. C. 575. The orphans' court may discharge from imprisonment a person held under an attachment issued by it: Kuntz's Est., 2 

Leh. 241. An attachment will be issued only at the instance of some one interested in the decree sought to be enforced: Patton's Est., 19 Super. 771

545. A petition for an attachment should be signed and sworn to by the party, not by his counsel: Chew's Est., 3 W. N. C. 392. And a formal order to pay should be entered and served before filing a petition for an attachment: Thomas's Est., 4 Kulp, 445. Est., 322 Pa. 394.

An attachment may issue against the person of a defaulting executor where, after the misappropriation of funds and his removal therefor, he has been declared a weak-minded person under the Act of May 28, 1907, P. L. 

292. Campbell's Est., 9 D. & C. 200.

Where an executor misappropriates assets of the estate on the theory that he was the owner thereof, and he was surcharged with the value, on petition for an attachment for contempt by nonpayment of the balance on the account to the legatee, the executor's answer that he is unable to pay because of his bankruptcy will be insufficient to prevent the issuance of an attachment. Wilt's Est. (No. 2), 46 York 133.

A person may be attached for contempt of court in failing to comply with an order against him, although such order has not been served upon him, if it appears that he has actual knowledge of the proceedings and of the order against him. Messmore's Est., 293 Pa. 63.

As to fi. fas. the act provides: "In case of a decree for the payment of money, against a party who has appeared, the complainant may have a writ of execution in the nature of a writ of fieri facias against personal property only, which writ may be allowed by the court, or by any judge thereof. "Such writs of fieri facias shall be directed to, and executed by the sheriff or coroner, as the case may require, of the proper county, and the proceedings thereon shall be the same as on writs of fieri facias against personal property issued by the court of common pleas of the same county." The petition should set forth the facts involved to show the jurisdiction of the court in the premises and the writ will be substantially similar to that in use in the common pleas.

Such writ may be awarded in favor of a guardian, to whom his ward's estate has been found indebted, on a settlement of his account: Shollenberger's App., 21 Pa. 337. A fi. fa. may issue out of the orphans' court, after a lapse of five years, without a revival of scire facias: Weyand's 

App., 62 Pa. 198. It may issue, notwithstanding an attachment has previously issued to enforce the same decree: Miles' Est., 4 Kulp. 152, 3

Lanc. Rev. 372, 3 Del. 88. But it may be set aside on petition showing that there is no necessity for execution: Ibid. The writ should recite enough of the record to support the order, particularly the decree, should be signed by the clerk of the orphans' court, and should direct that the writ and money made be returned to the orphans' court: Peckham's Est., 1 Kulp, 353, 10 Luz. L. Reg. 125.

The allowance of a fi. fa. is discretionary with the court, and when it is sought to compel payment of distributive shares while the auditor's report is in the supreme court on appeal, it will be allowed only in favor of such of the distributees as may protect the administrators by giving them proper and sufficient refunding bonds for restitution: Newhard's Est., (Ginginger's App.) 9 Dist. 764.

 302. PROCEDURE ON DEVASTAVIT, - ABSCOND- ING FIDUCIARY. 

The writ of attachment, of course, is ordinarily preceded by a citation issued on a petition to show cause. 

In case of emergency, however, immediate relief is provided: "When proof shall be made, on oath or affirmation, to the satisfaction of the court, or to any judge thereof, at the time of filing the petition as aforesaid, that the respondent has absconded or is about to abscond or depart from his usual place of abode, to the prejudice of the complainant, it shall be lawful for the court, or for such judge, to allow the issuing of a writ of attachment of the person, or a writ of sequestration, or both, in the first instance, against such respondent; and on the return thereof, the like proceedings may be had, as are authorized on the return of a citation." 24 

With equal expedition the respondent may secure dissolution of the writ: "If such attachment of the person or sequestration issued in the first instance be executed, the court, or any restitution of funds appropriated by him from the estate, will be discharged from custody upon transfer of such real and personal property as he may have, where the court is reliably informed that the defaulter, a man of advanced years, is suffering from two serious maladies which require special medical and surgical services, such as cannot be given in the county jail where he is confined. Niccolls's Est. (No. 2), 15 D. & C. 115.

Where, on petition for discharge from imprisonment of an executor committed for contempt in failing to comply with an order of the orphans' court directing him to pay over part of the balance on his account, the court was unable to find that the petitioner had done or was doing all that was within his means and ability to comply with the court's decree, the petition was refused. 

Where, on the hearing of a petition for the discharge from imprisonment of an executor committed for contempt in failing to comply with an order of the court to pay over moneys, it appeared that while the petitioner was liable to the estate for the moneys he was ordered to pay, he entered into an agreement with his wife under which he contended he and his wife were owners by entireties of personal property which he had purchased from himself as fiduciary and which he had not paid; that he and his wife were using this agreement as a means to withhold property from those to whom he was ordered to make payment; and that he had committed other acts showing that he had not attempted, in good faith, to purge himself of his contempt, the court dismissed the petition. Wilt Est. (No. 3), 47 York

Purd. Stat. Ann. Tit. 20, Sec. 2400. "It has been the rule in Pennsylvania for more than a century, a rule which we think should not be departed from, that each court is the exclusive judge of contempts committed against its process. 

When the court issuing the process has determined it has not been contemned, the appellate courts cannot decide otherwise. We said in Commonwealth v.

Yeates 2, where it refused to punish a contempt offered to the process of another court the judges asserting-so reads the report-"that they knew of no case where one court punished a contempt to another court, and they would not carry the system of punishment by attachment further than ''' In Williamthey were clearly warranted by practice and adjudged cases. son's Case, 26 Pa. 9, 18, Black, J., in speaking of the power in the courts, in proceedings for contempt says, "All courts have this power, and must necessarily have it, otherwise they could not protect themselves from insult, or enforce obedience to their process. Without it they would be utterly powerless. The authority to deal with an offender of this class, belongs exclusively to the court in which the offense is committed; and no other court, not even the highest, can interfere with its exercise.'' FINAL DECREE AND ITS REOPENING. 

A decree may of course be entered where the respondent does not appear in answer to the citation. "When a decree shall have been made against any party who shall not have appeared according to the requisitions of the citation, and a sequestration shall have issued against the real or personal estate of such party, the court may order the decree to be satisfied out of the estate and effects sequestered: Provided, That such order shall not be carried into execution, until the complainant shall have given security, to the satisfaction of the court, to abide the order of the court, touching the restitution of what he may have received, in case the respondent shall appear, and be admitted to defend the suit; but if such security shall not be given, the estate and effects sequestered, or the proceeds thereof, shall remain subject to the direction of the court, to abide its further order." 29

Notice of such order should be given the respondent. 

Opportunity is given to such respondent to appear and apply to have the decree opened: "If the party, against whom such decree shall have been made, or his representatives, shall, within one year after personal notice of such decree, and within five years after the entry thereof, when no such notice shall have been given, present a petition to the same court, praying to be admitted to be heard, and shall pay such costs as the court shall adjudge, the party so petitioning shall be admitted to a defense, and the case shall then proceed, in like manner as if such party had appeared in due season, and no decree had been made.'' 30

Such petition by the respondent should set forth in sufficient detail the prior proceedings resulting in the decree, a copy of such decree, a detailed outline of the defense of the respondent on the merits of the case, and concluding

CHAPTER XLVIII. 

WITNESSES AND EVIDENCE. 

307. SUBPOENAS. 

As is other courts of record, the attendance of witnesses may be compelled by proper process: 36 "Each of the orphans' courts of this commonwealth is empowered to issue writs of subpoena, under its official seal, into any county of this commonwealth, to summon and bring before the respective court, any person to give testimony in any cause or matter depending before it, under the penalties that are or shall be appointed and allowed in any such case by the laws of this commonwealth.'' 87

It will be noted that the power covers the entire state; may be used in any proceeding and the penalties are those in force under the general laws of the commonwealth. 

The right to subpoena is also given specifically to auditors, and probably by analogy to masters. 38

ORAL DEPOSITIONS OUTSIDE OF STATE. 

"Where the testimony of any witness is desired to be read in evidence in any proceeding now or hereafter pending in any orphans' court of this commonwealth, and such witness resides in any other state, territory or possession of the United States of America, or in any foreign country, the court may, on the application of any party, provide for the taking, in such other state, territory, possession or foreign country, of the testimony of such witness or witnesses orally, before an examiner appointed by the court, or before any person authorized by the laws of such other state, territory, possession or foreign country to administer oaths. In granting any such application the court may impose such terms as it shall deem proper, as to the payment by the party applying therefor of the costs and expenses involved, including reasonable counsel fees and traveling expenses, and may prescribe the notice to be given and the time within which such testimony shall be taken.” 46

The procedure is by petition, substantially in the form outlined in the preceding section.

313. TESTIMONY ON APPEALS FROM REGISTER. 

Special provision is made as to testimony on appeals from the register. Very frequently the testimony before the court would be an exact duplication of that before the register and hence its repetition would result in useless waste of time. The parties therefore may agree that the issue before the court be heard on the testimony before the register, as it is provided: "On appeal from the decision of any register of wills, or in proceedings removed from any register of wills by certification, the orphans' court shall hear the testimony de novo,52 unless all parties appearing in the proceeding shall agree that the case shall be heard on the testimony taken before such register: Provided, That in all cases the court shall have power to require the production before it, for examination, of the witnesses already examined, or of any other witnesses."' 53

314. ISSUES OF FACT IN GENERAL. 

We have already considered the subject of issues devisavit vel non,56 but the practice is by no means limited to such: "The orphans' court shall have power to send an issue to the court of common pleas56a of the same county for the trial of facts by jury, whenever they shall deem it expedient so to do." 58" 57 

56 See Sec. 29, supra. 

56a Under the Act of July 1, 1937 (P. L. 2665), which amends Sec. 21 of the Orphans' Court Act of 1917 (P. L. 363) the court may, at its discretion draw its own jury. The former act is amended, by adding at the end thereof a new subdivision to read as follows: 

"Section 21.-Jury trials by orphans' court. 

"(d) In any case where the orphans' court may deem it expedient or shall be required to send an issue to the court of common pleas for the trial of facts by a jury, the orphans' court, or a judge thereof, may, in its or his discretion, draw a jury, and a judge of said court shall preside at the trial of said issue. The panel of jurors drawn for service in the common pleas court of the county in which the orphans' court is located shall be available for such service in the orphans' court when required, and in counties where there is a separate orphans' court, the orphans' court and the courts of common pleas of said county shall, by appropriate rules, provide for and regulate the manner in which the jurors shall be made available and sent to the orphans' court when required for the trial of issues therein. "Unless and until the orphans' court otherwise directs, the appropriate rules of the common pleas courts of said county shall apply to jury trials of issues in the orphans' court, and matters relating to such trials shall be heard and disposed of by the orphans' court. 

The entry of judgments in such cases shall have the same force and effect and be subject to appeals in the same manner as appeals in like cases are now taken in the common pleas courts from judgments on issues certified by the orphans' court, except that only one appeal shall be taken and that shall be from the final decree of the orphans' court, upon which appeal all alleged errors may be assigned, whether arising in the jury trial or otherwise."

Under paragraph (a) of section 21 of the Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 

363, the orphans' court has a right to send any issues to the court of common pleas for the trial of facts by jury. The distinction between paragraphs (a) and (b) of this section is that the former provides for the voluntary action of the orphan's court. Paragraph (b) provides that a party may have the question of fact which arises determined by the verdict of a jury and he will be bound by it. This paragraph is for the benefit of the litigant; paragraph (a) is for the benefit of the court. 

The awarding of an issue under either paragraph (a) or (b) rests in the wise discretion and sound judgment of the court. 

Cross's Est., 4 Erie 38, 322; s. c. 3 Erie 273, 35 York 166.

When the orphans' court directs an issue to be certified on an appeal from the register and the issue is framed, no pleadings will be necessary. 

Whenever there is a certification to the common pleas, that court has exclusive jurisdiction, and the orphans' court is not informed what the jury did until return is made to it, and that return may be advisory or conclusive, and upon it the orphans' court bases its final decree. 

Where the findings on the issue are not conclusive, the orphans' court can refuse the advice they contain, and dispose of the matters involved as it may deem wise, despite the judgment of the common pleas. Coover's 

Est., 13 Erie 209.

Where there is a substantial dispute as to the ownership of funds or property between an administrator, who has never had possession of them, and one in possession claiming them as a gift from decedent, the orphans' court has no jurisdiction, but must grant an issue to the common pleas.

315. DISTRIBUTION OF PROCEEDS FROM SALE OF REAL ESTATE. 

Whenever real estate has been sold under decree of court and a question of fact arises as to distribution, it is provided: "Before an issue shall be directed upon the distribution of money arising from any sale of real estate made under order of the orphans' court, the applicant for such pleas, supported by such evidence, ought to stand. Connolly's Est., 20 

North. 348.

Where, in partition proceedings, there is nothing at issue except the construction of a paper, the matter is for the court alone and an issue will not be directed to the common pleas, as provided by Section 21 of the Act of 

June 7, 1917, P. L. 363, 382. Phillips's Est. (No. 1), 10 D. & C. 475.

The orphans' court has jurisdiction of a contest over a bank deposit which during the lifetime of decedent stood in the name of another as trustee for the decedent, such a deposit being on its face the property of the latter, and in the absence of evidence to show that it in fact belonged to another, the executor is entitled to the fund and chargeable with it. 

In such case, there is no substantial dispute which requires or justifies the grant of an issue to the court of common pleas. Greiner's Est., 15 D. & C. 12.

Tax appeals to the orphans' court are not governed by Section 21 (b) of the Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 363, because they are not appeals from any action of the register of wills, but from an appraisement made by an appraiser who is the agent of the Commonwealth. The right to such appeals is given and they are regulated by Section 13 of the Act of June 

20, 1919, P. L. 521.

There is no statute on practice warranting the award of an issue as of right in tax appeals. Wanamaker's Est., 8 D. & C. 569.

CHAPTER L. 

PARTITION. 

317. JURISDICTION OF . 

Where title by devise or descent vests in more than one person it is frequently desirable to separate the ownership in common to title in severalty in purparts of the whole. In such case jurisdiction is in the orphans' court, as it has been enacted that: "The orphans' court of each county of this commonwealth shall have jurisdiction," but not exclusive juris- 69 Partition is a possessory action, its purpose and effect being to give to each joint owner the possession he is entitled to of his share in severalty. 

Where the ownership is not in the plaintiff but in a trustee clothed with the title and charged with the management of the property it cannot be said that the plaintiff has a standing to ask for partition. Border's Est., 18 Berks 12.

In a partition proceeding, where an heir presents a petition for an inquest and another heir files an answer which avers "that the present market is not a satisfactory and suitable market on which to expose for sale the above premises" and that a "majority of the heirs desire that the property remain unsold," an Orphans' Court will grant the prayer of the petitioner. 

In such a case neither statement is sufficient to warrant a refusal of the prayer of the petition. 

The right of one heir to partition real estate held jointly with others is fundamental. Kauffmann's Est., 45 Lanc. 628, 30 D. & C. 607. 

70 See cases, 3 Purd. 3418, et seq. (a-z).

Where testatrix devises real estate to her five daughters, and further authorizes, directs and empowers her executrixes, for the payment of debts or otherwise, to sell all or any part of the estate, the executrixes may, by proper action, be compelled to make sale, but not by petition for partition by one of the devisees. Durning's Est., 7 D. & C. 592.

While there is no absolute statutory bar against the institution of partition proceedings in the orphans' court within one year from the date of decedent's death, under certain conditions such proceedings should be delayed until the expiration of that period, the matter being one largely within the discretion of the court to which the application is made. Kowala's Est., 21 D. & C. 77, 48 York 85.

A petition for partition is premature if it is filed before the estate is administered and debts paid a little more than a month after the death of the decedent. Breidigan's Est., 25 Sch. 377, 11 D. & C. 464. Rel'g on 

Clark's Est., 134 Pa. 140; Gallen's Est., 26 W. N. C. 308.

The right to partition of the real estate of a decedent among the persons entitled thereto may not be denied because under existing conditions the property is not readily marketable; if a sale becomes necessary, it is within the power and discretion of the court to refuse its approval unless in its judgment the price is adequate. Mayhew's Est. No. 1, 15 D. & C. 136. 797

13, 1840 (P. L. 320), 3 Purd. 3424, (v) which makes similar provision as to cases of testacy.

Both the orphans' court and the common pleas have jurisdiction to entertain partition proceedings, and where two actions are brought in different courts, the one which first acquires control of the controversy will retain it to the exclusion of the other. (Weil's Est., 45 Dauph. 105.)

82 The orphans' court has no jurisdiction to make partition of lands during a life estate when the life tenant is entitled to exclusive possession.

Where a widow, having a life interest in the whole of the real estate of her husband, conveys an undivided portion of such life interest to one of the remaindermen, the conveyance works a merger of the two estates, and as to such interest the remainderman takes a fee. 

In such case, as the remainderman has a present right of possession to the undivided interest so held in fee, he may maintain partition in the orphans' court, and the other remaindermen have no standing to object to it.

The orphans' court has no jurisdiction in partition to divide land where all the parties are not interested in all the land intended to be divided; if some of the parties have an interest in some of the land but not in another part, the partition is void. This act, like all other acts of assembly, must receive a reasonable construction. Its purport is that no person's rights be affected without due notice and an opportunity to be heard. It is essential that each person interested be named in the petition in order to make him a party. If he is not so named, he will not be bound by the proceedings.100 If everyone interested is so named, then all the parties will appear in the petition and writ, but it is not necessary that all the parties be named in the notice to each. It is clearly sufficient that each party be named in the notice to him. The insertion of the other names would be useless and therefore is not essential. The same reason applies to all interlocutory orders and decrees. In most of these, for instance in an order of sale, it would serve no purpose to name the parties interested. If the persons interested are named in the petition and thus made parties to the proceedings and receive actual notice of all steps taken as to which notice is required, the purpose of the act is accomplished and the manner in which it is done is immaterial.¹ 1

325. PROCEDURE WHERE PURPARTS DIFFER IN NUMBER FROM PARTIES ENTITLED. 

Frequently it is impracticable to divide the real estate into exactly the same number of shares as there are parties entitled thereto. Partition in the orphans' court of Pennsylvania is now under the Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 337. The power to partition land is either in commissioners or an inquest who, under section 8 of the act, allot purparts among the parties entitled in accordance with their respective interests, whether such interests be equal or otherwise, if the same can be done without prejudice to or spoiling the whole. This is a new section, declaratory of the existing law and introduced for the sake of completeness. 

The reasonable construction of the Act of 1917, P. L. 337, is that under section 8 the power of allotment by the inquest is final when confirmed by the court and there is no application to the court for a rule to accept or refuse under section 11. But when application has been made by any party in interest for a rule to accept or refuse purparts, the court, under section 11, is required to grant it. Galliford's Est., 85 P. L. J. 30, 50 York 

195, 28 D. & C. 606.

wherein a valuation shall have been made or shall be made of the whole or parts thereof, the same shall be allotted to such one or more of the parties in interest, whether entitled in possession or in remainder or to an undivided interest for life, and including the surviving spouse of the decedent, who shall, at the return of the rule to accept or refuse to take at the valuation, offer in writing the highest price therefor above the valuation returned; but if no higher offer be made for such real estate or any part thereof, it shall be allotted or ordered to be sold as herein provided.' 1926 When the parties are properly before the court, in obedience to the rule to accept or refuse, it is the first duty of the court to give each of them an opportunity of presenting one bid, in writing, for each separate purpart, in its order, if more than one, and no bid should be announced, or in any manner disclosed, until those present and desiring to do so, have handed in their bids on the purpart then being acted on. Then the bids should be opened by the court or by its direction, and the purpart bidden for forthwith announced to the party who offers therefor the highest price over the valuation. If two or more of the parties desire to submit a joint bid, there appears to be nothing in the act to forbid it, and, if their joint bid is the highest, the purpart should be awarded to them jointly. Each purpart, if there is more than one, should be taken up in its order, and disposed of in like manner. After all the parties, respectively, have thus had an opportunity of making a written offer for each purpart, and one or more purparts remain for which no bid is offered, they should be allotted according to the provisions of the act.27

Section 46 of the Act of 1832 provides that "when the decedent leaves no lineal descendants, the like proceedings shall be had in all respects, on the application of the persons in whom the estate shall vest in possession.''

Whether this means that the same order or priority is to be followed as among the lineal descendants seems not to have been decided. 

Section 8 of the Act of April 4, 1797, 3 Sm. L. 296, covered the case of the brothers and sisters.

In offering this section the Commissioners of 1915, in their report, said: "The Commissioners are of opinion that it is better to adopt the simple rule of seniority of age in all cases, whether the persons entitled are lineal descendants or other relatives of the decedent taking under the Intestate Law, or persons taking under his will, who may or may not be related to him."

Three methods of distribution are available where the property is allotted to distributees, that is by the court upon the submission of a distribution policy issued by a reputable title company, or upon the report of an auditors to whom the matter is referred for the purpose, or by the parties themselves, in which case mutual satisfaction pieces should be executed by all parties and filed of record in the proceeding. The determination of which of the above methods should be followed depends largely upon the amount of complications that may be involved; the willingness of the parties to agree upon the proper figures and the existence in the county of a title company qualified to issue its policy.

332. PROTECTION OF WIDOW'S INTEREST. 

47 

"Under Section 1 of the Act of April 8, 1833, P. L. 315, which applies to and controls the devolution of estates of intestates dying before December 31, 1917, a surviving widow was entitled to certain interests in her husband's real estate for life only, to wit, so-called statutory dower, i. e., a life estate in a third or a half part of such lands, depending on whether the decedent had left any children or issue. The Intestate Act of 1917, gives the widow of an intestate dying on or after December 31, 1917, not statutory dower as under the old law, but certain interests in fee simple in the decedent's real estate, to wit, an undivided one-third part thereof or an undivided half part thereof or more, depending on whether or not the decedent leaves children or issue, and if so, the number thereof. The Orphans' Court Partition Act had to be drafted by the law makers to meet the circumstances and requirements of estates of all intestates, to wit, those dying before, as well as those dying after December 31, 1917, for such act was to apply to estates of

334. PROVISIONS AS TO RENT DUE BY PARTIES IN POSSESSION. 

Frequently one or more of the tenants in common have been in possession of the premises. To prevent circuity of action for the rental due therefor, it is provided: "In case of partition of real estate now or hereafter held by two or more persons as tenants in common, where one or more of said tenants shall have been or shall hereafter be in possession of said real estate, the parties in possession shall have deducted from their distributive shares of said real estate the proportional part of the rental value thereof to which their co-tenant or co-tenants are entitled for the time such real estate shall have been in possession as aforesaid."' 50

341. APPOINTMENT OF AUDITOR TO ASCERTAIN LIENS, ETC. 

Frequently the share of some or all the parties entitled to the real estate are encumbered and lien claims and others of like nature arise. In order that the court may be properly advised of all such matters before final confirmation of the sale, it is provided: 93 "In all cases where, in consequence of proceedings in partition, the share, or any part thereof, of a party in interest, in real estate, shall be converted into money, either by reason of the impracticability or inequality of partition, or by virtue of a sale or otherwise, the orphans' court, before making a final decree confirming the partition or distributing the proceeds of sale, as the case may be, may appoint a suitable person as auditor," to ascertain whether there are any liens or other incumbrances on such real estate, affecting the interests of the parties. If it shall appear by the report of such auditor or otherwise, that there are such liens, the court may order the amount of money which may be payable to any of the parties against whom liens exist, to be paid into court, and shall have full power to decree the distribution thereof among the creditors or others entitled thereto. Where recognizance or other security shall be given for the payment of money, the court may make an order on the party giving such recognizance or other security, to pay the amount thereof into court, when the same shall become due, to be distributed in like manner among the persons holding liens at the time of the partition." 94

Provision is made for preliminary notice of such sale: "Before authorizing or directing any private sale of real estate under this act, public notice¹ thereof shall be given by advertisement printed in at least one newspaper, published in the county where such real estate is situated, and in such other papers as may be designated by the court, once a week for a period of three weeks prior to the date fixed by such order for authorizing or confirming such sale, and also written or printed notices, one of which shall be posted at a conspicuous place on the real estate proposed to be sold, and at least three of which shall be posted at three of the most public places in the vicinity of such real estate. 344. LANDS IN DIFFERENT COUNTIES. 

The procedure is of course more complicated where the real estate which is the subject matter of the proceeding is situated in different counties. Where the tracts adjoin it is provided: "When the lands, in respect to which application for partition shall be made to the orphans' court as aforesaid, lie in one or more adjoining tracts, in different counties, it shall be lawful for the orphans' court of the county in which the mansion house is situated, or, if there be no mansion house, the court of the county where the principal improvements may be, or, if there be no improvements, the court of either county, on the application of any person interested, either to proceed by the appointment of commissioners as aforesaid, or to issue its writ to the sheriff of the county within the jurisdiction of the court, specifying the lands of which a partition or valuation is to be made. Thereupon the said sheriff shall summon an inquest to divide or value the said lands, in the same manner as if the whole were within his proper bailiwick. Upon the return thereof, or upon the return of the commissioners appointed by the court, as aforesaid, the court may further proceed therein, in all respects as if all the said lands were in the county. Under the Act of June 7, 1917 (P. L. 337), relating to proceedings in partition, a partition does not become fixed or subject to the right of appeal until all the purparts have been awarded. 

This is the case because no definite determination can be properly reached as to any purpart until each and all of them have been finally considered.

CHAPTER LI. 

PROCEDURE UNDER REVISED PRICE ACT. 

347. RELIEF GRANTED AND JURISDICTION. 

Prior to 1853 relief in the sale or mortgage of real estate hampered by the provisions of a will or the incapacity of the owner was almost exclusively given by special acts of the legislature. 

In that year there was adopted the Price Act 24 which governed the practice and procedure in such cases until the passage in 1917 of the Revised Price Act,25 which practically reënacts the former act as amended by numerous intervening statutes. 

While, of course, it is really no part of a treatise on practice 25a to include at length any detailed consideration of subtantive law, yet the procedure under the act can scarcely be properly reviewed without an exact understanding of the relief that may be granted under the statute and the cases in which the court may grant such relief.

Obviously there will be considered herein only those cases which fall within the jurisdiction of the orphans' court.

WHAT RELIEF MAY BE GRANTED.

638), for the purpose.

The design of this act was to facilitate the transmission of titles, to make real property available for commercial and business uses, to encourage and promote improvement, and thereby to stimulate trade and develop the resources of the state; and it has no reference to or necessary connection with the administration of decedent's estates: Spencer v. Jennings, 123 Pa. 184. The object of the act is not to settle questions of title, but to transmit a title unincumbered by contingent or other interests: Hower's App., 55 Pa. 337 (4 Purd. 3997).

It is necessary in order for the court to reach a conclusion that a decree will be to the interest and advantage of those interested "that such facts shall be set out in the petition that will enable the court to form an opinion, such as the rental value of the property cost of maintenance in the way of repairs, taxes, water rent and other charges and such other facts as to dilapidation and decay, if any. It is not sufficient to say in the petition that it is to the interest of the minor that the sale be carried into effect. Such a statement is the opinion of the petitioner, which is, of course, of value, but it does not meet the requirements of the court which requires that the court shall conclude that it is for the best interest of the minor that the sale be made; and that conclusion can only be based upon facts contained in the petition, or by the taking of testimony before an auditor or the court." Scott's Est., 49 Pa. C. C. 295.

A petition will be refused which does not disclose the name of the proposed purchaser and is silent as to the fact that the sale can be made without prejudice to any trust, charity or purpose for which the real estate shall be held and without the violation of any law which may confer an immunity or exemption from sale or alienation. Scott's Est., 49 Pa. 

C. C. 295. 

See Oak Lane Bap. Ch. v. Brook, 1 D. & C. 199; Rorer's Est., 3 D. & 

C. 41.

No petition under the Price Act of 1917 may be allowed unless the court shall be of the opinion that a decree will be to the interest and advantage of all those interested therein. Irwin's Est., 77 P. L. J. 408.

Where it is to the interest and advantage of the parties interested the court, under this act, has authority to decree a sale of decedent's real estate against the objections of some of the living owners who are sui juris. 

Jefferies' Est., 37 Lanc. 435.

A purchaser of a right of way in real estate for and during the term of a life tenant only ought not to be compelled to be a party to a proceeding asking that the real estate be sold under the Price Act of 1917. In order to effect a sale of the land which will be advantageous to the remaindermen the life tenant must obtain the consent of her grantee to the sale and without it she cannot proceed and her petition was dismissed without prejudice to present the same either jointly as petitioner with the street railway company or with their consent. Irwin's Est., 77 P. L. J. 408.

It is not the privilege of a life tenant to allege in a petition for a sale under the Price Act that an advantage may arise from a sale for something in which she no longer has any interest, or, in other words, unless she is able to present for sale the very thing in which she was given a life interest. The remaindermen cannot be subjected to a sale of their interest unless they or the purchaser can obtain possession of all the interest owned by the life tenant and themselves and a life tenant will not be permitted to say that an advantage can arise unless that advantage springs from a sale of the whole. The disposal of a part destroyed her right to allege a present advantage arising from a sale of the whole, because possession cannot be given during her lifetime. Irwin's Est., 77 P. L. J. 408.

§ 348 

348. GENERAL PROVISIONS. 

Similarly as a guide to practice it may not be amiss to call attention to certain general provisions of the statute as affecting its scope and effect. 

Existing laws, rights and powers are not impaired: "Nothing herein contained shall be taken to repeal or impair the authority of any act of assembly, general or private, authorizing the sale of real estate by decree of court or otherwise, nor to affect or impair any rights or powers, otherwise existing in any person or corporation to do any of the acts which the court is empowered to authorize or confirm under the provisions of Section 1 of this act.'' 54

The person to execute the decree depends upon the status of the title and the order of the court: "In all cases where, under the provisions of this act, sales, mortgages, leases, or conveyances on ground rent shall be authorized or directed, the same shall be made by executors, administrators, guardians, trustees, committees or owners having a present vested interest, or trustees appointed for the purpose, as the court may order.'' 55

Where the proceedings shall be for the purpose of freeing the title of any limitation or defeasibility hereafter described, and that purpose shall be set forth in the petition in addition to the explanation of the title, then: "Every such decree made by the court shall have the once been active has ceased and determined."'

Hence, title held under a declaration of trust whereby the legal owner agrees to convey the real estate "unto any person or persons named and designated-upon request or requests-made-in writing" by the equitable owner, who subsequently died, is not held under a trust contemplated by this section. The trust here is passive. All possible purposes of the trust ended on the death of the equitable owner and title then vested in her heirs or devisees whose remedy is by partition. Behringer's Est., 265 Pa. 111. See also Myers v. Crick, 271 Pa. 399.

METHOD OF PROCEDURE. 

The proceedings are of course instituted by petition." 

A complete outline of the method to be followed is given by the act: 

"All jurisdiction conferred by this act on the orphans' court or the court of common pleas shall be exercised on the petition of any party in interest" supported by oath 66 As to the county where such petition shall be presented, the act provides: "In all proceedings under the provisions of this act, where the real estate shall lie wholly within one county, the petition shall be presented only in the court of that county.' 

Revised Price Act of 1917, (P. L. 388) Sec. 19, (a) which is a new clause in accordance with the proviso to Sec. 1 of the Price Act of 1853. (See Purd. Stat. Ann. Tit. 20, Sec. 1565.) "When an application shall be made, under the provisions of this act, for the sale, mortgaging, leasing or other procedeings relating to real estate, through which real estate the line dividing two or more counties runs, the court of the county in which the mansion house is situated, or, if there be no mansion house, the court of the county where the principal improvements may be, or, if there be no improvements, the court of either county may exercise jurisdiction as to the whole of such real estate, irrespective of the county line; and any such sale, mortgaging, leasing or other decree relating to real estate, shall be as effectual as if the whole of such real estate had been within the county whereof said court has jurisdiction. Notices of said proceedings, as required by this act, shall be given in all the counties in which the land is situated, and a certified copy of all proceedings shall be filed in the proper court of each county in which said land is situated. Any mortgage taken to secure the purchase money, or any part thereof, shall be duly recorded in each of the counties in which said lands lie, as required by law." 

Revised Price Act of 1917 (P. L. 388), Sec. 19 (b), which is derived from Sec. 1 of the Act of May 28, 1915 (P. L. 635), 6 Purd. 7286, supplementary to the Price Act. The last two sentences have been made uniform with the provisions of Section 16 (1) 2 of the Fiduciaries Act (see 100, supra). See also Purd. Stat. Ann. Tit. 20, Sec. 1566. 

67 An administrator has no standing to petition the orphans' court for leave to sell real estate where there are no debts and the purpose of the sale is stated to be for the best interests of the minor heirs of the decedent. Zimmerman's Est., 41 York 111, 75 P. L. J. 911, 9 D. & C. 564.

The Revised Price Act is not intended to divest estates without consent of the owners, but to provide the means for the regulation of the sale where the joint owners disagree as to the control and disposition of the property.

Where a petition by a trustee for the sale of real estate under the Revised Price Act contains no averment as to any such disagreement and there is no sworn statement alleging any such lack of agreement, the court will assume that no such disagreement exists. * *

Though the orphans' court has jurisdiction to sell real estate in any of the cases recited in the act, it is plain that it cannot exercise jurisdiction until a proper case is presented, at the suit of a proper person, and then only to the extent to which that person has a right to demand its exercise:

350. PUBLIC SALES,-NOTICE, CONFIRMATION. 

Naturally one of the principal requisites of a public sale is adequate notice, and as to this it is provided: "Whenever, by the provisions of this act, it shall be lawful for the court to order the public sale of real estate, public notice of such sale shall be given by the person who is to make the sale, once a week for a period of three weeks before the day appointed therefor, by advertisement in at least one newspaper published in the county, if there be one, or if there be none, then in an adjoining county; and in all cases, notice shall also be given by handbills, one of which shall be posted at a conspicuous place on the real estate proposed to be sold, and at least three of which shall be posted at three of the most public places in the vicinity of such estate." 351. PRIVATE SALES. 

For cause shown a private sale may be authorized" or 

"The courts of the several counties of this commonwealth, in all cases where, under the provisions of this act, such courts have power to order the sale of real estate, may authorize or direct a private sale, if, in the opinion of the court, under all the circumstances, a better price can be obtained at private than at public sale, as where the interest shall be undivided, or for any other sufficient cause. 99 77 

76 See Forms Nos. 298-306, App., pp. 332-360, for various petitions under this clause of the act. 

77 Revised Price Act of 1917 (P. L. 388), Sec. 20 (a), copied from

In a proceeding for a private sale of real estate the petition must show that a day for hearing had been fixed and proof must be made that notice of such sale had been given in the manner required by law; the court must be convinced that a better price can be obtained at such private sale than at public sale. "We have of record an order which in effect directs the private sale of the real estate to Kreger, and it is here proposed that another order shall be made directing the sale of the same real estate to Blew. This is not good practice. The rights of Kreger to this real estate which he acquired by reason of the order already made should not be rescinded without notice. "It does not appear upon the record before us that the advertisement required by law has been made or that the parties in interest have had their day in court. "The order obtained upon the original petition is not in accordance with our practice or the law because it appears to direct a sale. The proper practice is to fix a day for hearing, and the act requires that before directing a private sale, the court shall require proof by affidavit to be filed in the proceeding that notice of such sale has been given in the manner required by law, and shall be of the opinion under all the circumstances, a better price can be obtained at private than at public sale. 

Moyer's Est., 70 P. L. J. 686.''

When there is no direction in the will to sell real estate and no necessity for the payment of debts is asserted the executors have nothing to do with the real estate.

When the interest of a minor in real estate is to be sold the guardian is the proper party to make sale. Gottschall's Est., 20 Sch. 372.

A life tenant of real estate cannot, by private sale, convey anything more than her life estate.

In such case, the orphans' court properly exercises its discretion in refusing to approve the sale of the whole fee to the proposed purchaser, where a much larger price is offered by another party. Hays's Est., 286 Pa. 520.

SALE OR MORTGAGE TO FIDUCIARY. 

From the nature of the case where the fiduciary making the sale or mortgage is also the purchaser or mortgagee special safeguards are thrown around the trans

"Whenever any court, having jurisdiction under this act to decree a sale or mortgage of real estate, shall issue its order to any executor, administrator, guardian or trustee, specially appointed for the purpose or otherwise, to sell or mortgage such real estate, and shall, in any case within its jurisdiction, give authority to any executor, administrator, guardian or trustee, to bid at such sale, and shall confirm the sale to such fiduciary or shall authorize the making of such mortgage to any executor, administrator, guardian or trustee, the said court may make an order directing its clerk to execute a deed or mortgage, as the case may be, for said real estate to such purchaser or mortgagee, who shall give security and shall account for the amount of said purchase money or mortgage money, in the settlement of his accounts, to said court.'' 84

Where a trustee takes title to realty for his personal benefit, whether in his own name or that of another, when such title could and ordinarily would have been taken in the name of the trust estate, the beneficiaries have the option of holding him liable for any profit he may make, or for the value of the estate's interest in the property, with interest thereon; but this rule does not apply where he thus takes title for the benefit of the estate itself, and properly accounts to it for all sums received from the use and sale of the property. 85

CHAPTER LII. 

ESCHEAT. 

357. WHEN ESCHEAT OCCURS. 

It has been noted that the estate of a decedent who dies intestate 98 or where a partial intestacy is involved through any defect in the will" descends to and is distributed to his heirs and next of kin. 

It occasionally happens however that no such heirs or kindred can be found or are known. In such case the law provides: "In default of all such known heirs or kindred or surviving spouse, competent to take as aforesaid, the real and personal estate of such intestate, [shall go to and be vested in the commonwealth by escheat] remaining after the payment of all just debts and legal charges, shall be sold by the executor or administrator of the estate, and the net proceeds of such sale shall be, by him, paid into the State Treasury for the use of the commonwealth. 

Such sale shall be made only under the supervision of the court having jurisdiction of the estate, and in accordance with the laws of the commonwealth providing for the payment into the State Treasury of unclaimed funds in the hands of fiduciaries. 100

CHAPTER LIII. 

ADOPTION. 

363. JURISDICTION. 

"It cannot be said that adoption is germane to the jurisdiction of the Orphans' Court. Notwithstanding its name, the Orphans' Court is not a court of orphans or a children's court or a court of domestic relations, as some may ignorantly suppose. It has nothing to do with children as such. It deals with the estates of decedents and the fiduciaries entrusted with them and the estates of minors and their guardians. It is an estate court, or better, a fiduciaries' court; its proper province is the contest of wills and their construction, the settlement of decedents' estates and the appointment, supervision and control of fiduciaries and the like subjects. When this court appoints guardians for minor children it establishes a fiduciary relation, but the care of minors and the supervision of their welfare are foreign to our duties. By adoption, however, no fiduciary relation is established; there is a change of status, the person adopted is taken out of the family of its natural parents and transplanted into the family of the adopting parents, and it should be remembered that by the statute adults may be adopted as well as minors, in which case the impropriety of the jurisdiction is even more manifest. The whole matter of adoption, indeed, is unknown to the common law; it is imported from the Roman jurisprudence, where adoption and adrogation formed an important head of the law for reasons not now or here applicable. 

"It should be remarked that it has been the policy of this Commonwealth from colonial days to limit the functions of this court to the settlement of estates and the control and appointment of fiduciaries. The specialization thereby afforded to the court has enabled it the better and more expeditiously to distribute estates among creditors, heirs and legatees. Every one in the State eventually becomes either a decedent, heir, legatee or creditor, and, hence, it is of the utmost importance to the whole community that the work of this court should be 886

$ 887 

IG handled with accuracy and expedition rather than that there should be added to its functions the granting of petitions for adoption; a jurisdiction very foreign to the specialization mapped out by the public policy of this 

Commonwealth.

A child may be adopted over the objection of the parent where the parent has abandoned the child.

If by reason of misfortune the parents are compelled to turn over the child either to public or private charity, with settled purpose to forego all parental duties and relinquish all parental claims, and if some other person assumes the parents' claims and duties, the court may be warranted in the conclusion that within the meaning of the Act of Assembly there has been an abandonment; particularly if the child is of years of discretion and desires the adoption by the person or persons who have performed all of the ties and fulfilled all of the obligations of the parents; and if the adoption is manifestly for the best inuterests of the child. 

A decree of adoption was made over the objections of the mother where it appeared on the hearing that the father deserted his wife and children, and that the mother, by reason of her poverty unconditionally delivered the child to another, who delivered her to the petitioner and his wife, who for over thirteen years cared for, supported and educated the child wholly at their own expense, without any contribution by the mother, that the child frequently visited the mother, at the expense of the petitioner and the mother visited the child seldom during those years; that the child was well educated and capable of determining her own destiny, and, while professing filial affection for her mother, desired to be adopted by the petitioner; that the parental custody of the child by her mother would not be for the child's best interests or consistent with her welfare; and that the objection of the mother to the adoption where wholly capricious. Moul's 

Adp'n, 50 York 205.

Under the provisions of the act the consent of a parent to the adoption of a child by another is not necessary where the parent had abandoned the child. Williams' Pet'n, 74 P. L. J. 170.

Bonnem's Ad'n, 8 D. & C. 146, 74 P. L. J. 705.

The inducement to decrees for all adoptions must be the welfare of the children. The State is always interested and concerned for their cultural development, their religious, moral, physical, intellectual and material uplift, and its power to control these and prevent depravity by adoption cannot be stayed by an arbitrary refusal of consent by a parent, who, being able to support his children, has refused to do so and left them to drift. 

Beech's Ad'n, 74 P. L. J. 49, 7 D. & C. 505.

In proceedings in the orphans' court for the adoption of an orphan minor child, the paramount question always to be considered by the court is the best interests and welfare of the child, and unless it can be found by the court, under all the circumstances of the particular case, the court will refuse to grant the prayer of the petition. Sweeney's Adoption, 35 Lack. 22. 

Where both maternal and paternal grandparents are desirous of adopting their grandchildren and are equally able and willing to provide for them, the best interests of the children should govern the decision.

Wash. 54, 40 York 188.

Where a man adopts the son of his wife by a former marriage, the wife joining in the proceedings as natural mother but not as wife of the adopting parent, at a time when the wife had separated from her husband and returned to her former husband, and thereafter the son dies leaving real estate, the title thereto of relatives of the adopting father (who predeceased the son) is not so clear as to be good and marketable in an action between such heirs and a prospective purchaser; but the validity of the title must await determination in an action to which the natural mother is a party. Fisher v. Green, 28 D. & C. 195.

18. Oaths to Execution of Will Not Signed Because of Extremity of Last Illness. 

COUNTY OF ADAMS. SS: 

about Before me, the subscriber, register of wills in and for the county aforesaid, personally came A. B. and C., all of the borough of

Adams County, Pa., who being severally sworn, do depose and say that they have been long and intimately acquainted with D., the above named testator of 

Adams County. That on the morning of o'clock, D., being in the extremity of his last illness, requested A. to write his will in the presence of B. and C. as the witnesses thereto whom he requested for that purpose; that the said A. got paper and pencil and wrote down the foregoing as the will of the said D. as he dictated it just as it is therein written; that after it was thus written it was read by A. to said D. and he was asked whether that was what he wanted and he said yes; and while it was being prepared

APPENDIX 

for signing by the said D. he became unconscious and in a dying condition, wholly insensible, and died in less than half an hour. That he was prevented by the extremity of his last illness and dying condition from signing the same or giving directions that the same should be signed for him; that at the time of dictating his will as aforesaid, and afterwards, when the same was read to him and he answered that that was right, it was what he wanted, the said D., was of sound and disposing mind, memory and understanding, and knew all about the disposition of his property which he had made. That when the will was ready he was not only incapable of signing the will but also of directing it to be done by another for him; that this will was made in his own dwelling house where he had resided for many years immediately preceding his death. That his death occurred morning about o'clock. That the dictation of the foregoing will and the reducing of it to writing and the reading of it to D. and his answer that it was all right, it was what he wanted was all in the presence of the undersigned B. and C. as witnesses, and that said testator was then fully conscious of what he was doing, but suddenly became insensible and in a dying condition and wholly incapable of signing it or directing it to be signed. 

Sworn and subscribed, etc.

A. B. C.
