DECREE. 

 192-, прои consideration of the annexed petition, a citation is awarded, directed to (names) to show cause why the ap- * If such facts and circumstances appear to be prima facie sufficient a citation will be granted: Rule 5, Sec. (B), Phila. Co. Petition not supported by averments of fact will be dismissed: How's Estate, 21 Dist. 493.

In certain counties, notably in Philadelphia, "the rules of court require that where an appeal has been taken from a decision of the register of wills, the appellant's petition for a citation shall set forth the facts and circumstances upon which he replies" and "where fraud, misrepresentation or undue influence is charged, not only should the names of the persons who committed the unlawful acts be stated, but, in addition, the acts and things done and said by such persons, with the facts and circumstances of time and place connected therewith should be set out; otherwise the averments are mere conclusions of law without facts upon which to base them, and are, therefore, insufficient to give the court jurisdiction; in other words the petition should set out facts which, if proved, would be sufficient to make a prima facie case justifying the award of an issue, except, perhaps, in cases where the burden of proof has shifted because of the existence of a confidential relation."' Gummey, J., in Kris' Est., 29 

Dist. 447. See also Wright's Est., 9 Pa. C. C. 235, 27 W. N. C. 372.

A party not cited may set aside the verdict of a jury: Miller's Estate, 166 Pa. 97.

The court will not hear testimony until return of service on all parties has been made, and, if an answer filed, until the cause has been put at issue by replication.

34. Form of Precept to Common Pleas Under Section 21(b) of Orphans' Court Act. 

"(L. S.) 

COUNTY. SS: 

"THE COMMONWEALTH OF PENNSYLVANIA: 

To the Judges of the Court of Common Pleas of the said 

County, greeting: day of in "WHEREAS, A. B., on the in the year, etc., presented to G. H., our register of wills of said county, for probate, a certain writing hereto annexed, purporting to have been made the- day of the year, etc. (or otherwise describing the paper in question), which said writing the said A. B. avers is the last will and testament of the said C. D., and whereas E. D., who is a son and heir of the said C. D. (or intermarried with F. D., who is a daughter and heir, etc., according to the fact), hath objected before our said register that the said writing was procured by duress and constraint (stating the matters of fact objected), and whereas our said register hath admitted (or refused to admit) said writing to probate as the last will and testament of the said C. D., and whereas the said E. D. hath appealed from the decree of our said register to our orphans' court for the said county (or as the case may be), and whereas the said E. D. (or A. B.) hath requested that an issue may be directed into our said court of common pleas to try by a jury the validity of the said writing, and the matters of fact which may be objected thereto in our said court; therefore, we command you that you cause an action to be entered upon the records of our said court, as of the day of the delivery of this our precept into the office of the prothonotary of our said court, between the said A. B. and the said E. D., so that an issue therein may be formed upon the merits of the controversy between the said parties, and tried in due course according to the practice of our said courts in actions commenced by writ; and further, that you cause all other persons who may be interested in the estate of the said C. D., as heirs, relations or next of kin, devisees, legatees or executors, to be warned, so that they may come into our said court and become party to the said action, if they shall see canse, and that you certify the result of the trial so had in the premises into our said orphans' court. 

"Attest. I. J., President Judge of the Orphans' Court of the said county.

64. Form of Exceptions to Master's Report. 

In the Orphans' Court of Philadelphia County. 

In re estate of 

CHARLES EDWARD JONES, a presumed decedent. :} 

October Term, 1922, 

No. 520. 

AND NOW, to wit, April 5, 1923, WILLIAM J. JONES by his counsel, -, Esq., excepts to the report of 

RUFUS MARSHALL, Esq., Master, for the following reasons: 

1.

The Learned Master erred in his finding of fact as follows: 

"That as the said CHARLES EDWARD JONES, the presumed decedent, has been absent from his last known residence, to wit: Chicago, Illinois, and unheard from since 1875, which absence has been unexplained or other-

APPENDIX 

wise accounted for, a legal presumption of his death seven years thereafter (1882) has been fully established in accordance with the provisions of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, P. L. 460, Section 6 (a), (c), (d)." 

2. The Learned Master erred in not finding as a fact that the said CHARLES EDWARD JONES, a presumed decedent, has been absent from his last known residence, to wit: Chicago, Illinois, and unheard from since July, 1912, which absence has been unexplained or otherwise accounted for. 

3. The Learned Master erred in not finding as a fact that a legal presumption of the death of the said 

CHARLES EDWARD JONES seven years thereafter, to wit: July, 1919, has been fully established in accordance with the provisions of Section (c) of the Fiduciaries 

Act of 1917. 

Attorneys for WILLIAM J. JONES.

82. Form of Petition for Leave to Join in Incorporation of Decedent's Business. 

 April Term, 1922,  

No. 2345.

The petition of JANE DOE respectfully represents: 

1. That JOHN DOE died March 19, 1922, intestate, a resident of Philadelphia County, and letters of administration were granted on his estate to your petitioner by the Register of Wills of Philadelphia County on May 15, 1922. 

2. That the only persons interested in the decedent's estate are your petitioner, his widow, and GEORGE DOE, his son, a minor nineteen years of age, for whose estate the UNITED TRUST COMPANY has been ap pointed guardian. 

3. That among the assets of the said decedent is an undivided one-half interest in the partnership or firm of DOE & ROE. The other member of the said firm is 

PETER ROE, who is living and of full age. The said partners at the time of the death of the decedent and for ten years prior thereto had been engaged in business as antique furniture dealers at No. 1131 Liberty Street, Philadelphia, which they occupied under a lease. The physical assets of the said business if sold at a forced sale would probably not bring over the sum of $5,000, which after the payment of the outstanding accounts would be reduced to the sum of approximately $3,000, to which the estate of said decedent is entitled to onehalf. If the said business can be continued as a going concern, however, and the assets disposed of in the usual course of business, a much greater price will be realized therefrom. In fact as your petitioner is informed and believes they would bring more than double their appraised value. 

4. That GEORGE DOE, the minor son of decedent for two years prior to his father's death was employed as a clerk in the said business with the intention on the part of the said decedent that he should learn the busi-

APPENDIX 

ness and ultimately take his father's place as a member of the said firm, as his father was advancing in years and desired to retire as an active partner in said business. 

5. That PETER ROE, the surviving partner of the said firm, is willing to incorporate the said business under the laws of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania for the sum of $5,000, and it has been suggested, subject to the approval of the orphans' court, that the entire assets of the said business be transferred to the said corporation if and when formed in consideration of the issuance of the stock of the said corporation, to wit: 100 shares at the par value of $50 each, one-half to the said PETER ROE and one-half to your petitioner as administratrix of the said JOHN DOE, deceased, to be held and accounted for by her as part of the assets of the said estate. 

6. That the formation of this corporation in the manner set forth will not prejudice the rights of any creditors or any persons interested in said estate.

8. That your petitioner, not for the purpose of delay, but believing an injustice had been done in levying the tax as aforesaid, appealed from the act of the Register of Wills in assessing the tax as above set forth and has duly entered security as required by law for the payment of said tax in the event of his failure to prosecute the said appeal to a successful conclusion, and the record of said appeal has been duly remitted to your Honorable Court. 

6. Your petitioner avers that the Register of Wills of erred in assessing the tax as above set forth as ten per cent for the following reasons: (1) The Act of Assembly in effect at the date of the deed of trust, was the Act of May 6, 1887, (P. L. 

79) whereunder the rate of tax is fixed at five per cent. (2) The Act of Assembly in effect subsequent to the date of the said deed of trust, but prior to the date of the death of the said life tenant was the so-called "Transfer Inheritance Tax Act" of June 20, 1919, (P. 

L. 521) wherein the collateral transfer inheritance tax was fixed at five per cent and the amendatory Act of May 4, 1921, which increased the rate of taxation on transfers to collaterals from five to ten per cent. (3) At the time of the execution of the deed of trust there was no collateral tax at the rate of ten per cent, the rate, at that time being five per cent, and therefore the interest in remainder passing to your petitioner was not subject to collateral tax at the rate of ten per cent, even though it vested in possession after the passage of the Act of May 4, 1921, increasing the rate to ten per cent. 

(4) The Register of Wills erred in assessing col lateral tax at the rate of ten per cent under the Act of May 4, 1921. (5) The Register of Wills erred in not assessing collateral tax at the rate of five per cent under the Act of 

May 6, 1887 (P. L. 79).

APPENDIX 

Wherefore your petitioner prays that a citation be issued directed to the Honorable, Register of Wills of, to show cause why the appeal of from the appraisement for transfer inheritance tax purposes dated on the estate of deceased, at the rate of ten per cent should not be sustained and the said rate of tax reduced from ten per cent to five per cent. 

 (Affidavit.) 

A. D. 

 upon consideration of the annexed petition and on motion of -, attorneys for the petitioner, the prayer of said petition is granted and a citation is hereby directed to be issued to the Honorable, Register of Wills of to show cause why the appeal of from the appraisement for transfer inheritance tax purposes dated on the estate of deceased, at the rate of ten per cent should not be sustained and the said rate of tax reduced from ten per cent to five per cent.

II. ACTS RELATING TO  I. Act of February 18, 1824′ (8 Sm. L. 194). 

An Act to enable executors, administrators, guardians and other trustees, to invest their trust money. 

1. If any executor, administrator, guardian or trustee shall have in his hands money, the principal whereof is to remain in his possession, and the interests to be paid. or accumulate, he may apply to the Orphans' Court, who may direct an investment in the debt of the U. S., of 

Pennsylvania, of the City of Philadelphia, or in real securities, at such prices or on such rates of interest and terms of payment as the court shall think fit, and if the money is so invested, the executor, &c., shall be exempt from liability for loss on the same, in like manner as if such investment had been made in conformity to the directions of the last will or other instruments creating the trusts, or by a law of this state. Nothing herein to authorize the court to make a direction contrary to any will or other instrument. 2. So much of the Act* of 1713, 1 vol. 83, establishing Orphans' Courts, contrary hereto as hereby supplied, repealed.

NOTE: This and the next two paragraphs are a combination of Section 14 of the Act of March 29, 1832, 1 Purd. 1109, Section 2 of the Act of April 13, 1854, P. L. 369, 1 Purd. 1110, and Section 1 of the Act of May

The Commissioners believe that the powers of investment granted to fiduciaries under the present law are too greatly restricted and that their enlargement would be welcomed throughout the State. At present trustees are limited to loans of the United States, the State of Pennsylvania, municipal corporations of the State, mortgages and ground rents; and according to the literal wording of the statutes the decree of the orphans' court should be first obtained, although in practice the statutes have been considered as authorizing the investments specified, and the necessity of a preliminary application has been disregarded. 

The Commissioners would be willing to recommend a more extensive act were it not for the Constitution, which in Art. III, Section 22, would seem to prohibit the legislature from authorizing an investment in the bonds or stocks of a private corporation. They have, however, drafted this section so as to include investments in bonds of municipal corporations in other states, requiring, in such instances, a preliminary application to the court for authority to make such investments.

The division into three paragraphs has been made for the purpose of clearness. The investments enumerated in paragraph 1 are made legal investments without application to the court. Explanatory Note: The text of the foregoing Act is printed in the form prescribed by the Act of May 16, 1923, P. L. 11. In accordance with the provisions of that act, the words, phrases or provisions striken out or eliminated from the former law by the adoption of the amendment are enclosed between brackets [ ], and all the new words, phrases or provisions inserted into or added to the law by the passage of the amendment are printed in italics.

The reader, therefore, in order to ascertain the correct meaning, status and interpretation of the law as changed by the amendatory statute, should omit the words, phrases or provisions within brackets, and should read and interpret, as part of the new statute, the words, phrases, or provisions printed in italics. The matter in brackets has been retained for the sole purpose of enabling the reader to discern more readily the changes made in the former law, and to compare it with the law as enacted.

The Act was drafted under the supervision of the Committee on Trust Investments of the Pennsylvania Bankers Association, and was finally enacted and approved in substantially the form recommended by the committee.

It will be noted that this Act is in form, an amendment of paragraphs 

1, 2 and 3 of Section 41 (a) of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917. The Fidu ciaries Act only applies to "executors, administrators, guardians and trustees, whether domiciliary or ancillary, subject to the jurisdiction of the Orphans' Court of any county of this Commonwealth," and accordingly the application of the present Act is likewise restricted. 

However, the Committee on Trust Investments also sponsored a companion Act, (P. Hence, the present Acts will now control all investments by all fiduciaries.

11 References: Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, Sec. 41 (a)

Comments: (1) Prior to the adoption of this Act, the Fiduciaries Act authorized the investment of trust funds “in first mortgages on real estate in this Commonwealth, securing bonds or other obligations not exceeding in amount two-thirds of the fair value of such real estate. "" Several members of the Committee on Trust Investments, and others who were consulted, were of the opinion that this provision was inadequate, and accordingly, the Committee recommended that it be revised and amplified as it appears above in the Act, the Legislature having followed the Committee's recommendation. As revised and amplified, the sub-section makes several changes in the prior law. (2) The requirement that the real estate covered by the mortgage shall be "improved" is new, and adds an additional safeguard for investments of this character. (3) The provision limiting investments of this character to mortgages payable not more than five years after date, but permitting investments in long term mortgages provided 60% of the principal amount of the mortgage is to be amortized over a period not exceeding 20 years is also new, and represents a further effort to provide additional safety for trust investments, and at the same time, to authorize investments in mortgages created pursuant to the Federal Housing Act, or similar legislation. (4) The remaining new provisions were recommended for the purpose of clarifying the prior law, and probably add no requirement not heretofore voluntarily observed by fiduciaries in making such investments.

1, 20 P. S. 801.

The above provision adds the requirement that the real estate shall be improved, and the further restriction that the rental, capitalized at 5%, shall not exceed % of the fair value of the real estate out of which the ground rent issues.

APPENDIX Subsection (6). Real Estate Bonds.-Bonds of one or more individuals or corporations, secured by improved real estate, situated within this Commonwealth, not including real estate used as a theatre or for manufacturing purposes, conveyed by mortgage or deed of trust to a corporation organized under the laws of the United States or of this Commonwealth and authorized to act as trustee for all such bondholders, which mortgage or deed of trust shall be a first lien upon the real estate so conveyed. Such bonds shall be payable not more than twenty years after the date thereof, and the mortgage or deed of trust securing them, shall contain a provision for the annual reduction of the principal amount of the bonds secured thereby, in an amount equal to at least two per centum of the maximum amount of the bonds outstanding at any time prior to the date of the investment by the fiduciary, plus an amount equal to the interest on all bonds previously retired by such annual reductions.

The total amount of any such bond issue shall not exceed two-thirds of the fair value of the real estate securing such bonds, and, at the date of such investment, there shall not be any default in the payment of any matured principal or interest on such bonds, or in any annual reduction of the principal amount of such bonds, as provided in the mortgage or deed of trust securing such bonds.

If the date of the investment is subsequent to the original date of the mortgage securing the bonds or to the date of any renewal or extension thereof, such investment being made by purchase, assignment, or otherwise, no new appraisement shall be necessary to fix the fair value of the mortgaged property at the date of the investment in such mortgage bonds by such fiduciary: 

Provided, That such an appraisal, as is provided herein, has been made within three years from the date of such investment, and a reputable person familiar with real estate values in the vicinity of the mortgaged property and also familiar with such previous appraisement shall certify in writing that, at the date of such investment, the face amount of the bonds secured by such mortgage does not exceed two-thirds of the fair value of the mort-

gaged property. Any such certificate shall be filed and preserved among the records of the fiduciary. 13 

Subsection (7). Fractional Interests.-Fractional un divided interests in any investment in which a fiduciary is authorized by this section to invest trust funds or in a pool or fund of such investments established and being maintained by any trust company or bank and trust company in its trust department as may be provided by law, such fractional interests being apportioned among estates of which the person or corporation creating such fractional undivided interests in the fiduciary. 

In the case of an investment is a fractional interest in a mortgage or in a pool or fund containing mortgages, if the date of such investment is subsequent to the orig- 

13 References: Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, Sec. 41 (a) 

Banking Code-Act of May 15, 1933, P. L. 624, Art. XII, Sec. 1208 A (8), 7 P. S. Pocket Supp. 819-1208 A (8). 

Comments: (1) This section makes several changes in the prior law. 

The prior law authorized investments in "bonds . . of one or more individuals

As a result of this provision, there arose the familiar practice of transferring the property, which was to be mortgaged to secure bonds, to an individual "straw man," who created the mortgage, issued the bonds, and immediately transferred the property back to the corporation, which assumed the mortgage and the bonds. Obviously, under this practice, the provision restricting investments to bonds of individuals afforded no additional protection to the investor. The Committee therefore recommended that bonds of corporations should be made legal investments to avoid the "straw man" practice. (2) The provision requiring the real estate covered by the mortgage to be improved is also new, and is in accordance with the changes made in sub-sections (4) and (5) noted above. (3) The exclusion of bonds secured upon "real estate used as a theatre or for manufacturing purposes" is also new, and it was suggested that hotels, churches, apartment buildings and other properties which might be termed “single purpose properties' should also be excluded. However, it was thought that the exclusion of all such properties would eliminate many sound investments, but that the exclusion of real estate used for manufacturing purposes should be retained, thus eliminating so-called “industrial bonds," because of the additional hazards attendant upon a manufacturing business. (4) The requirement that the mortgage or deed of trust securing the bonds shall contain a provision for the amortization of bonds is also new and is deemed advisable in view of the recent history of bonds of this character. (5) The paragraph concerning the appraisal of real estate upon which such bonds are secured is likewise new in this Act, and is designed to avoid unnecessary, repeated appraisals of the same property, but at the same time, to provide adequate protection in this respect for trust investments.

Subsection (8). Railroad Obligations.15-Railroad ob ligations, subject to the following provisions: (a) As used in this subsection, the words "qualified railroad corporation" shall mean a railroad corporation 

14 References: Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, Sec. 41 (a) 

Comments: (1) Under the prior law, a trustee was permitted to invest in trust certificates issued by a trust company certifying that the holders thereof are respectively the owners of undivided interests in deposits with such trust company of securities in which trust funds may be invested. . . ." 

This provision was revised in the above section to eliminate the necessity for a formal trust certificate. The purpose of the provision is to permit investment in fractional interests in a legal investment, or in a pool or fund of such investments, and there would seem to be no advantage in requiring the investment to be evidenced by a formal trust certificate, providing the investment is properly apportioned among two or more trust estates and evidenced either by a trust certificate, an assignment, memorandum, or otherwise.

Comments: This entire subsection, relating to railroad obligations, follows generally the provisions of the New York Banking Law. It was believed, however, that since obligations of this character were being made legal investments for trust funds for the first time in this Commonwealth, a conservative policy should be adopted, and for this reason, several ad-

other than a street railroad corporation which, at the date of the investment by the fiduciary, meets the following requirements: (1) It shall be a railroad corporation, incorporated under the laws of the United States, or of any state, or Commonwealth thereof, or of the District of Columbia; (2) It shall own or operate, within the United States, not less than five hundred miles of standard-gauge railroad line, exclusive of sidings; (3) Its railroad operating revenues, derived from the operation of all railroad lines operated by it, including leased lines and lines owned or leased by a subsidiary corporation, all of the voting stock of which, except directors' qualifying shares, is owned by it, for its fiscal year next preceding the date of the investment, shall have been not less than fifteen million dollars; (4) The sum of the total amount of its outstanding fully paid capital stock, plus the total amount of its outstanding obligations not containing an unconditional promise to pay interest thereon, shall, at the close of its fiscal year preceding the date of the investment by the fiduciary, or, if there has been a public offering of securities since the close of its last fiscal year, then after the necessary adjustments have been made therefor, be not less than one-half of the total amount of its obligations ditional limitations and restrictions have been added to the basic provisions of the New York law.

Comments: The policy of the New York law, upon which this section is based, is to secure a safe investment by providing that the railroad company issuing the bonds to be made legal investments shall be a strong company. The preceding six paragraphs contain the provisions guaranteeing the strength of the railroad company and the tests therein set forth are substantially the same as the tests prescribed in the New York law and the law of certain other states. 

It is to be noted, however, that in paragraph (6), special provision has been made to cover the years of the depression and during such years, a railroad company can qualify if its earnings have been equal to its fixed charges, with a year of grace. After 1935, however, the company's income available for fixed charges will have to be at least equal to 1½ times its fixed charges, allowing also for a year of grace. This provision is more severe than the New York law where an amendatory act was adopted, the effect of which is to eliminate entirely from consideration the depression years. It was believed, however, that such a provision was too liberal and that even in depression years, the railroad companies whose bonds are to be made legal investments should have established a reasonably satisfactory record.

18 Comments: (1) It is the theory of this subsection relating to railroad obligations that, not only should trust investments be restricted to obligations of strong companies, but that in addition, the obligation itself should provide conservative security for the investment. The provisions set forth in paragraph (b) are designed to attain the latter result. The requirement in the paragraph (b) (2) (A), that a part of the railroad lines covered by the mortgage shall constitute a part of a through route between two or more communities each of at least 40,000 inhabitants as determined by the preceding U. S. census is a new thought first suggested in the present bill. The purpose of the test is to admit as qualified railroad obligations only those obligations which are a first lien on mileage having a satisfactory earning power. A careful analysis of all railroads meeting the other requirements of this section indicated that the application of this practical test would qualify only railroad obligations, the earning power securing which was deemed satisfactory, and consequently, this test was adopted in lieu of a test based directly on traffic density, which would necessarily have been technical and difficult of application. (2) Paragraph (b) (2) (C), relating to equipment trust certificates is substantially in accordance with the New York law. The principal change made in this Act is the limitation of the amount of the equipment trust certificates to be issued to 75% of the value of the equipment, the New 

York provision being 80%.

25 References: National Housing Act of June 27, 1934, c. 847, 48 Stat. 

1246, 12 U. S. C. A., Sec. 1701 et seq. 

Comments: The inclusion of mortgages insured by the Federal Housing 

Administrator is, of course, new in the present Act. Title II of the National Housing Act, cited above, authorizes the Federal Housing Administrator to insure certain mortgages, and further provides that if a mortgage so insured becomes in default, the mortgagee, after foreclosure, may convey the property to the Administrator, who is then required to issue debentures to the mortgagee in an amount equal to the value of the mortgage and make an adjustment with respect to certain other items, such as the costs of foreclosure, etc.

The debentures bear interest at the rate fixed by the Administrator when the mortgage was insured, and, in general, are payable only out of the special "Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund" established by the Act. The 

Act provides, however, "that debentures issued in exchange for mortgages insured prior to July 1, 1937, shall be fully guaranteed as to principal and interest by the United States.'' Consequently, it was deemed advisable to include, as legal investments for trust funds, only mortgages insured prior to July 1, 1937, and the debentures issued in connection therewith.

Subsection (19). General Provisions- 

(a) Nothing contained in this section shall be construed to relieve any fiduciary from the duty of exercising due care and prudence in the performance of the duties of his office. 29 (b) Nothing contained in this section shall be construed to authorize any fiduciary to make any investment contrary to the directions in regard to investments contained in the will, deed, or other instrument creating the trust in his care, nor to limit or restrict the authority conferred upon any such fiduciary with respect to investments by any such instrument.30 (c) No fiduciary shall be liable for any loss incurred with respect to any investment not legal for the investment of trust funds, as provided in this section, when such nonlegal investment was received by such fiduciary pursuant to the terms of the will, deed, decree of court, or other instrument, or, if such nonlegal investment was legal when received, or when the investment was made by the fiduciary: provided such fiduciary exercises due care and prudence in the disposition or retention of any such nonlegal investment.3: 31 (d) Within the meaning of this section, the term "fair value" of real estate shall be the value placed thereon in a written appraisement by two reputable persons, familiar with real estate value in the vicinity of such real estate, who shall actually have inspected the property 29 Comments: This provision is a statement of the law, as established by court decisions, prior to the adoption of the present act, although no such specific provision was contained in the Fiduciaries Act in its prior form. It was deemed advisable to include this statement of the rule so that the present act would, to a certain extent, serve as a code of the law relating to the investment of trust funds for the guidance of fiduciaries.

To this provision has been added the statement that nothing in the act shall be construed to limit the authority conferred upon the fiduciary by any such instrument.

XI. Act of July 2, 1935 (P. L. 540). 

AN ACT 

Defining the term "fiduciary" prescribing the nature and kind of investments which may be made by such fiduciaries validating certain investments heretofore made by such fiduciaries and repealing acts and parts of acts inconsistent herewith. 

Section 1. Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania in General Assembly met and it is hereby enacted by the authority of the same. That the term "fiduciary" as used in this act shall include guardians, committees, trustees and other fiduciaries whether domiciliary or ancil-

APPENDIX 

lary subject to the jurisdiction of the court of common pleas of any county of this Commonwealth. 

Section 2. Any such fiduciary holding moneys to be invested may invest such moneys in any investment in which at that time a fiduciary subject to the jurisdiction of the orphans' court of any county of this Commonwealth may invest like moneys.

Section 3. When any such fiduciary shall have in his hands any moneys to be invested as aforesaid he may present a petition to the court of common pleas having jurisdiction of his accounts, stating the circumstances of the case and the amount or sum of money which he is desirous of investing, whereupon it shall be lawful for the court upon due proof aided if necessary by the report of a master to make an order directing the investment of such moneys in real estate in this Commonwealth other than ground rents or in the bonds or certificates of debt now created or hereafter to be created and issued according to law by any other state of the United States or by any of the counties or cities of such other state at such prices or on such rates of interest and terms of payment respectively as the court shall think fit: Provided, That no such investment shall be directed unless it shall be the opinion of the court that it will be for the advantage of the estate and no change be made in the course of succession by such investment as regards the heirs or next of kin of the cestui que trust: And provided further, That nothing herein contained shall authorize the court to make an order contrary to the directions contained in any deed of trust or other instrument in regard to the investment of such moneys.

Section 4. (a) When any such fiduciary shall have invested any such moneys as authorized herein or as authorized by any court of common pleas as herein provided such fiduciary shall be exempted from all liability for loss on the same in like manner as if such investments had been made in pursuance of directions in the deed of trust or other instrument creating the trust, it being hereby declared that all such investments are legal investments of moneys by such fiduciaries. (b) No fiduciary shall be liable for any loss incurred with respect to any investment not legal for the invest-

ment of trust funds as provided in this act when such nonlegal investment was received by such fiduciary pursuant to the terms of the deed, decree of court or other instrument, or if such nonlegal investment was legal when received or when the investment was made by the fiduciary, provided such fiduciary exercises due care and prudence in the disposition or retention of any such nonlegal investment. (c) Nothing contained in this act shall be construed to authorize any fiduciary to make any investment contrary to the directions in regard to investments contained in the deed or other instrument creating the trust in his care nor to limit or restrict the authority conferred upon any such fiduciary with respect to investments by any such deed or other instrument. (d) Nothing contained in this act shall be construed to relieve any fiduciary from the duty of exercising due care and prudence in the performance of the duties of his office.

Section 5. All acts or parts of acts inconsistent here with are hereby repealed.

Section 6. This act shall become effective immediately upon final enactment.

APPROVED-The 2d day of July, A. D. 1935.

Section 1107. Any Officer Authorized to Take Oath.- 

In any case in which the laws of this Commonwealth require that a fiduciary shall take an oath or affirmation, or execute an affidavit, any officer of a bank and trust company or trust company, which is acting in such fiduciary capacity, shall be authorized to take such oath or affirmation, or execute such affidavit, on behalf of such bank and trust company or trust company. 33

Section 1109.84 [Mortgage or] Securities Pools for In vestment of Fiduciary Funds.-A. A trust company, or a bank and trust company in its trust department, may establish a pool or fund of [bonds secured by mortgages, or of other] securities, purchased solely with funds of estates held by it as fiduciary. All [the bonds secured by mortgages, and all] the securities, which comprise such pool or fund, shall be of the class authorized as legal investments for funds held by fiduciaries. The bank and trust company or the trust company shall apportion fractional undivided interest in such pool or fund to estates of which it is fiduciary in the proportions in which their funds were used to purchase [the bonds secured by mortgages, or] the securities, which comprise such pool or fund. Interests in such pool or fund shall not be sold to any corporation or person, but shall be held solely by the bank and trust company, or the trust company as fiduciary, and the equitable interest owned solely by the estates of which such bank and trust company or such trust company is fiduciary. Interests in such pool or fund may be transferred in distribution to any beneficiary, and, in order to make distribution, may be sold by such bank and trust company or trust company to another trust estate or estates of which it is fiduciary, or, it may be sold by a bank and trust company, to its commercial department, which may in turn resell the same to another trust estate or estates of which it is fiduciary, but not to any other corporation or person. 

B. Such bank and trust company or such trust company shall designate clearly upon its records the names of the estates on behalf of which such bank and trust company or trust company as fiduciary owns a fractional undivided interest in such pool or fund, and the extent of the interest of the estate therein. No such estate shall
