Section 2. Following section 1109 of the said act, as herein amended, and before section 1110 of the said act, six new sections numbered 1109-1, 1109-2, 1109-3, 1109-4, 1109-5, and 1109-6 are hereby inserted and added to the said act as follows: 

Section 1109-1. Investment of Fiduciary Funds in Undivided Interests in Bonds Secured by Mortgages or in Other Securities.-A. A bank and trust company in its trust department or a trust company may create undivided interests in any single bond secured by a mortgage or in any single security, to be apportioned among estates of which it is fiduciary. Any such bond secured by a mortgage and any such security shall be of the class authorized as legal investments for funds held by fiduciaries. The bank and trust company or the trust company shall create and assign such undivided interests in a bond secured by a mortgage or in a security to estates of which it is the fiduciary in the proportion to which their funds were used to purchase such asset. Interests in any such asset shall not be sold to any corporation or person, but shall be held solely by the bank and trust company or the trust company as fiduciary, and the equitable interests owned solely by the estates of which such bank and trust company or such trust company is fiduciary. Interests in any such asset may be transferred in distribution to any beneficiary, and may be sold by such bank and trust company or trust company to another trust estate or estates of which it is fiduciary, or, in order to make distribution, may be sold by a bank and trust company to its commercial department, which may, in turn, resell the same to another trust estate or estates of which it is fiduciary, but not to any other corporation or person.

B. Such bank and trust company or such trust company shall designate clearly upon its records the names

APPENDIX 

of the estates on behalf of which such bank and trust company or trust company, as fiduciary, owns a fractional undivided interest in any bond secured by a mortgage or in any such security, and the extent of the interests of such estates therein. No such estate shall be deemed to have individual ownership of any such bond secured by a mortgage or any such security, but shall be deemed to have an undivided interest therein. 

The bank and trust company or the trust company may issue a certificate of participation for every estate on behalf of which such bank and trust company or trust company, as fiduciary, owns a fractional undivided interest in any such bond secured by a mortgage or in any such security. Such certificate shall state on its face that it is issued without guarantee by the issuing bank and trust company or trust company of the payment of either principal or interest, and that it will be paid only when funds become available out of any such bond secured by a mortgage or any such security. It shall also state any other important condition governing such situa tion.

C. This section shall not be construed to affect fractional interests in any such bond secured by a mortgage or in any such security, created by a bank and trust company or a trust company prior to the third day of July, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-three.

Section 1109-2. Establishment and Maintenance of 

Mortgage Investment Funds.-A. A bank and trust company in its trust department or a trust company may establish and maintain one or more mortgage investment funds in which it may invest only the funds of estates held by it as fiduciary. Interests in any such fund shall not be sold to any corporation or person, but shall be held solely by the bank and trust company or the trust company, as fiduciary, and the equitable interests therein owned solely by the estates of which such bank and trust company or such trust company is fiduciary. 

B. Such bank and trust company or such trust company shall not invest the funds of any such mortgage investment fund, except as follows:

(1) In mortgages of one or more individuals or corporations securing bonds or other obligations subject to the following provisions: 

(a) At the date of the recording of any such mortgage in the office of the recorder of deeds of the proper county, or at the date of any extension or renewal thereof, such mortgage shall meet the following requirements: (1) Such mortgage shall contain an unconditional promise to pay interest on the bonds or other obligations secured thereby, and shall be or become a first lien upon improved real estate, including improved farm lands, situated within this Commonwealth prior to all other liens, except taxes previously levied or assessed, but not then payable, and except taxes then due and payable or delinquent for the payment of which taxes, provision has been made in the mortgage settlement. (II) The unpaid principal amount of the bonds or other obligations secured by such mortgage shall not exceed two-thirds of the fair value of such real estate. (III) Such mortgage shall be payable not more than fifteen (15) years after the date thereof, or the date of any renewal or extension thereof, and shall provide either for the annual reduction of the principal amount of the bonds or other obligations secured thereby in an amount equal to at least five per centum of the unpaid principal amount of such mortgage on the date thereof, or on the date of any renewal or extension thereof, the amount of the required annual reduction payment may be made payable in installments, but such installment payments shall be required to be paid not less frequently than semi-annually, or such mortgage shall provide for the amortization of the total unpaid principal amount of such mortgage on the date thereof, or the date of any renewal or extension thereof, by the payment of a fixed amount each month during the term of such mortgage, or the term of any renewal or extension thereof, such monthly payments being fixed at an amount which will include the interest due on such mortgage on the date of such payments, and an additional amount to be applied in the reduction of the unpaid principal amount of such mortgage, which additional amounts will provide

APPENDIX 

for the amortization of the unpaid principal amount of such mortgage during the term thereof, or the term of any renewal or extension thereof, as herein provided. (b) At the date any such mortgage is acquired by the mortgage investment fund such mortgage shall also meet the following requirements: 

(I) All interest previously due thereon, if any, shall have been paid in full to the next preceding interest payment date as therein provided. (II) No taxes levied or assessed upon the property covered thereby upon which any penalty has accrued shall then remain unpaid, unless provision for the payment thereof is made at the date of the acquisition thereof by the fund. (III) The unpaid principal amount of the bonds or other obligations secured by such mortgage shall not exceed two-thirds of the fair value of the mortgaged property. (c) A mortgage investment fund shall not contain any mortgage securing bonds or other obligations, the unpaid principal amount of which exceeds ten thousand dollars, unless the total book value of all the assets in any such fund exceeds two hundred thousand dollars, in which event the fund may contain mortgages securing bonds or other obligations, the unpaid principal amount of which does not exceed five per centum of such total value or fifty thousand dollars, whichever amount is the lesser. (d) The term "fair value" of real estate shall mean the value placed thereon in a written appraisement by two reputable persons familiar with real estate value in the vicinity of such real estate who shall actually have inspected the property before making the appraisement, and shall so certify therein. Any such appraisement shall be filed and preserved among the records of the fiduciary. (2) In mortgages of one or more individuals or corporations upon improved real estate, including improved farm lands, situated within this Commonwealth securing bonds or other obligations insured by the Federal Housing Administrator prior to the first day of July, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-seven, pursuant to the

provisions of Title two of the National Housing Act, approved the twenty-seventh day of June, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-four, or thereafter insured by such administrator with like force and effect pursuant to any amendment, revision or extension of the provisions of the said act. At the date of the investment in any such mortgage, the said insurance thereon shall be in full force and effect. (3) In the event that mortgages in which the moneys of the mortgage investment fund may be invested cannot be obtained, any such moneys available for investment may be temporarily invested in the following securities, bonds or obligations, either bearing interest, or sold on a discount basis of the United States or the United States Treasury, or those for the payment of the principal and interest on which the faith and credit of the United States is pledged, including such bonds or obligations of the District of Columbia, or in bonds or other interest-bearing obligations of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, or those for payment of the principal and interest on which the faith and credit of the Commonwealth is pledged. However, the amount invested in such securities shall not exceed twenty per centum of the total book value of all the assets contained in any such fund, and as soon as mortgages in which the moneys of the mortgage investment fund may be invested can be obtained, such securities shall be sold and the proceeds invested in such mortgages.

C. No further investment of the moneys contained in any such fund shall be made when the amount of cash contained therein, excluding cash consisting of income, shall be less than five per centum of the total amount of all outstanding participations in the fund. 

D. No mortgage shall be acquired by the mortgage investment fund until such mortgage has been reviewed by the board of directors of such bank and trust company or trust company, or by a duly authorized committee of such board, including at least two members thereof, and approved by the board or such committee as a proper investment for inclusion in such fund. Similarly no moneys of such fund shall be invested in other securities

APPENDIX 

until such board of directors, or such committee thereof, has determined that no mortgages, in which the moneys of the fund may be invested, can be obtained, and has approved of the investment in such securities as a proper investment of the moneys of such fund. All such reviews and approvals of mortgages and determinations and approvals of other investments shall be recorded in the minutes of the meetings of such board of directors, or of such committee thereof.

E. The real estate upon which each mortgage contained in any such fund is secured, and any real estate contained in the fund, except real estate secured upon mortgages of one or more individuals or corporations securing bonds or other obligations insured by the Federal Housing Administrator prior to the first day of July, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-seven, pursuant to the provisions of Title two of the National 

Housing Act, approved the twenty-seventh day of June, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-four, or thereafter insured by such administrator with like force and effect pursuant to any amendment, revision or extension of the provisions of said act, shall be appraised at least once every three years by two reputable persons appointed by the board of directors of such bank and trust company or trust company familiar with real estate values in the vicinity where any such real estate is situated, who shall actually have inspected such real estate and shall so certify in such appraisement. Any such appraisement shall be filed and preserved among the records of the fiduciary. 

Section 1109-3. Investments of Fiduciary Funds in Mortgage Investment Funds.-A. The total amount of the funds of any one trust estate invested in a mortgage investment fund shall not exceed one thousand dollars or two per centum of the total book value of all the assets contained in any such mortgage investment fund, whichever amount is the greater. Such bank and trust company or such trust company shall designate clearly upon its books and records the names of the estates the funds of which have been invested in such fund, and the total amount of the funds of such estates so invested. No such estate shall be deemed to have individual ownership of any mortgage, security or other asset contained in any

such fund, but shall be deemed to have an undivided interest in the fund, the incidents of such ownership being as herein set forth.

The bank and trust company or the trust company may issue a certificate of participation for every estate on behalf of which such bank and trust company or trust company as fiduciary owns an undivided interest in such fund. Such certificate shall state on its face that it is issued without guarantee by the issuing bank and trust company or trust company of the payment of either principal or interest, and that it will be paid only when funds become available out of the bonds secured by mortgages or out of the securities comprising the fund. It shall also state any other important condition covering such situation.

B. Such bank and trust company or such trust company may sell and transfer participations in any such fund from one estate of which such bank and trust company or trust company is the fiduciary with any other person or corporation to any other such estate, or, in order to make distribution, such participations may be sold by a bank and trust company to its commercial department, which may, in turn, resell the same to another trust estate of which it is the fiduciary, but not to any other corporation or person.

C. Except as herein otherwise provided, upon the termination of any trust estate the funds of which have been invested in any such mortgage investment fund, such estate or the beneficiaries thereof shall be entitled to receive in cash the total amount of the funds of such estate invested in such fund with the income thereon determined, as herein provided, to the date of such payment, but such income shall not be paid until the amount thereof shall have been determined on the next accounting date, as herein provided. However in the event that, upon the termination of any such trust estate, there shall not be available sufficient cash to pay the amount of its participation in the fund, such bank and trust company or such trust company may issue withdrawal certificates of participation in the fund for the amount of such estate's participation in the fund not paid in cash. Such certificates shall state that they may be redeemed by the

APPENDIX 

mortgage investment fund at any time, and they shall be so redeemed as soon as funds are available for such purpose. Such certificate shall also state that it is issued without guarantee by the issuing bank and trust company or trust company of the payment of either principal or interest, and that it will be paid only when funds become available out of the bonds secured by mortgages or out of the securities comprising the fund. It shall also state any other important condition covering such situation. Until redeemed, the owners of any such withdrawal certificates shall be entitled to distributions of income from the fund, as herein provided. So long as any such certificates are outstanding, no further investments of the moneys contained in the fund shall be made, and no new investment therein shall be made of the funds of any estate of which such bank and trust company or such trust company is the fiduciary, as herein provided. 

In the event any such mortgage investment fund is closed and placed in liquidation, as herein provided, while any such withdrawal certificates are outstanding, the holders thereof shall receive no preferences, but shall have the same rights as the owners of other participations in such fund. 

Section 1109-4. Management of Mortgage Investment 

Funds.-A. A bank and trust company or a trust company maintaining a mortgage investment fund shall invest and reinvest the moneys of such fund as herein provided, collect the income arising therefrom, and, at least semi-annually, it shall determine the net income of the fund during the period since the last determination thereof. 

B. Such bank and trust company or such trust company shall establish and maintain a reserve account as an integral part of the fund. At the close of each earning period, if the total amount contained in such reserve account is less than ten per centum of the total amount of all outstanding participations in the fund, such bank and trust company or such trust company shall transfer to such reserve account out of net income of the fund such amount as the bank and trust company or the trust company, in its discretion, shall determine to be proper under the circumstances, but the total of the amounts so

to be transferred to the reserve account during any year shall not be less than one-half of one per centum nor more than one per centum of the average of the total amounts of all outstanding participations in the fund at the close of each earning period. 

C. The balance of the net income remaining after transferring such part thereof to the reserve account, as herein provided, shall thereupon be distributed among the owners of the outstanding participations in the fund, and the owners of withdrawal certificates of participation, in proportion to the amounts of their participations and the period of time owned.

D. When any such mortgage investment fund shall have acquired the real estate upon which any mortgage contained in the fund was secured, either by the foreclosure of any such mortgage or otherwise, such mortgage shall be removed from the fund's mortgage account, and the real estate so acquired shall be transferred to the fund's real estate account. Upon the subsequent sale of any such real estate, the gain or loss shall be the difference between the sale price and the value at which such real estate was carried in the fund's real estate account. Any such loss shall be charged against the reserve account and any such gain shall be credited to such reserve account.

E. Upon the sale of any security contained in such fund, the bank and trust company or the trust company shall determine the gain or loss thereon, being the difference between the sale price and the book value thereof. Any such loss shall be charged against the reserve account and any such gain shall be credited to such reserve account.

Section 1109-5. Closing and Liquidation of Mortgage 

Investment Funds.-A. A mortgage investment fund may be closed by a bank and trust company or a trust company at any time by resolution of its board of directors, regularly adopted and duly recorded in the minutes of the meetings of such board of directors. 

B. A mortgage investment fund shall be closed when either of the following conditions exist: (1) When the sum of the following items, less the amount of the reserve account, exceeds ten per centum

APPENDIX 

of the total book value of all of the assets contained in any such fund: (a) The total amount of unpaid principal of all mortgages contained in the fund upon which any interest remains due and unpaid for six months after such interest became due and payable. (b) The total amount of unpaid principal of all mortgages contained in the fund which are secured upon real estate upon which taxes have been levied and assessed, which remain unpaid for six months after such taxes have been, or could have been, certified as delinquent by the proper taxing authority. (c) The total amount of unpaid principal of all mortgages contained in the fund upon which the unpaid principal amount exceeds two-thirds of the last appraised value of the mortgaged real estate, and such unpaid principal amount has not been reduced by the amount of such excess within six months from the date of such last appraisement. (d) The total amount of the book value of all of the real estate contained in the fund. (e) The excess of the book value of any securities contained in the fund over the current market value of such securities. 

In determining the sum of the foregoing items any mortgage which could be included either in item (a), (b) or (c) shall only be included in one of such items, and all mortgages securing bonds or other obligations insured by the Federal Housing Administrator in which moneys of such fund may be invested as herein provided, shall be excluded from the said items if the insurance on such mortgages is in full force and effect. (2) When the total amount of unpaid principal of all mortgages contained in the fund upon which any amortization payment remains due and unpaid for a period of six months after such payment became due exceeds twenty per centum of the total book value of all the assets contained in such fund. However, when amortization payments totalling twenty-five per centum of the principal amount secured by any such mortgage have been made, such bank and trust company or such trust company may permit the suspension of further amorti-

zation payments for a period not exceeding two years, and in such event, any such mortgage during the period of such suspension shall not be included in determining the total amount of this item. 

C. When a mortgage investment fund, created after the effective date of this act, is closed as herein provided, no further investments therein shall be made, and the bank and trust company or the trust company shall file a petition for the liquidation of such fund in the court which has theretofore exercised jurisdiction over it, or if no court has yet exercised such jurisdiction, then in the court of common pleas or the orphans' court of the county in which the principal place of business of the institution is located. Such petition shall set forth the closing of such fund, the reasons therefor, and other pertinent facts. Such notice of the filing of such petition shall be given and such hearings shall be had thereon, as such court may direct, and such court shall thereupon determine whether the fund should be liquidated, and shall either authorize such liquidation or make such other order as it shall deem necessary or advisable for the protection of all parties in interest. 

If the court authorize the liquidation of any such fund, the bank and trust company or the trust company shall continue to collect the income therefrom and to determine and distribute the net income thereof semi-annually, as herein provided, and when it shall have accumulated sufficient funds available for the payment of the principal of outstanding participations and withdrawal certificates of participation, it may, and when such accumulated funds equal ten per centum of the total amount of all such participations and certificates, it shall distribute such funds among the owners of such participations and certificates. All such distributions of income and principal shall be made among all owners of participations and withdrawal certificates of participation in the fund, as of the date such fund was closed, in proportion to the amounts thereof, and in the case of income, in proportion to the period owned. Upon final liquidation, if all of the owners of such participations and withdrawal certificates of participation have been paid in full, and any funds remain undistributed, including any balance in the re-

APPENDIX 

serve account, such funds shall be regarded as principal, and shall also be distributed among the owners of such participations and certificates in proportion to the amounts thereof.

D. When a mortgage investment fund has been closed, either before or after the effective date of this act, the bank and trust company or the trust company or any other party in interest may petition the court for an order directing the payment of all or a part of any participation or withdrawal certificate of participation in advance, or on other than a pro rata basis in cases of emergency or necessity, or by any such petition may submit to the court a plan for the liquidation of the fund and the payment of such participations and withdrawal certificates in any manner which may be deemed necessary or advisable under the circumstances. Any such petition shall set forth all the pertinent facts, and such notice of the filing thereof shall be given and such hearings thereon shall be had, as the court shall direct. Thereupon the court may direct such payment or approve such plan or enter such order as it shall deem fitting and proper under the circumstances, having due regard for the protection of the owners of all participations and withdrawal certificates of participation.

Section 1109-6. General Provisions.-Except as herein otherwise specifically provided in this act, the provisions hereof relating to mortgage investment* funds shall be applicable to any such fund hereafter established and to any pool or fund containing mortgages heretofore established by any bank and trust company or trust company. 

Any such mortgage investment fund or pool or fund containing mortgages which does not conform to the provisions of this act, shall be closed, and no further investments therein shall be made, and, in the case of any such mortgage investment fund hereafter established, such bank and trust company or trust company shall proceed to liquidate such fund as provided in this act. 

Section 1110. Prohibition upon Lending Fiduciary 

Funds to Officers, Directors, or Employes.—A bank and trust company or a trust company shall not lend either *"'inventment" in the original.

directly or indirectly, to any director, officer, or employe of such bank and trust company or trust company, or to any director, officer, or employe of any affiliated institution or affiliated national banking association, as defined in this act, any funds which it holds as fiduciary, except such funds as it holds as fiduciary for such director, officer, or employe, and except for loans made upon the security of a mortgage upon the home of such director, officer, or employe.

For the purpose of this section, a loan shall be considered to be granted to a director, officer, or employe, when such loan is made for the benefit of such director, officer, or employe, or to or for the benefit of a partnership or other unincorporated association of which such director, officer, or employe is a partner or a member. A loan shall be deemed to be granted for the benefit of a person, partnership, or other unincorporated association, or corporation to the extent that the proceeds of such loan are credited to or transferred to such person, partnership, other unincorporated association, or corporation. Every director, officer, or employe granting such loan on behalf of the bank and trust company or the trust company, and every director, officer, or employe wilfully accepting such loan with knowledge that it was granted in violation of the provisions of this section, shall be guilty of a misdemeanor, and shall, upon conviction thereof, be subject to imprisonment for a period not exceeding one year, or a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars or both; he shall also be subject to a further fine of a sum equal to the amount of loan so granted, or received, and shall forever thereafter be disqualified from acting as a director, officer, or employe of any institution in this Commonwealth. 19

III. CASES. 

ARISING UNDER PENNSYLVANIA RULE OF APPORTIONMENT OF EXTRAORDINARY DIVIDENDS, ETC. 

(a) In Appellate Courts. 

Earp's App., 28 Pa. 368 (1857).

Allocation as between principal and income of large surplus profits by a manufacturing company above current dividends reflected in new stock issued to estate several years after decedent's death. 

McKeen's App., 42 Pa. 479 (1862).

Specific gift to wife as income of "the yearly dividend of my interest in the wire factory, in South Easton . . .” precluded apportionment of dividend declared Jan. 1st after decedent's death and same awarded entirely to widow. 

Wiltbank's App., 64 Pa. 256 (1870), 7 Phila. 327.

Proceeds of sale of rights to subscribe and profits on sale of stock subscribed held as "a mere product of an advantage belonging" to the stock, and, in the latter instance, as a "profit" or "premium" and payable to life tenant. 

Moss's App., 83 Pa. 264 (1877).

Where a corporation having a surplus of earnings increased its capital stock and executor holding 100 shares sold 60 rights and with the proceeds bought 40 new shares at par, the latter were awarded to principal and not to the life-tenant entitled under the will to "the income, profits and products" for life. 

Biddle's App., 99 Pa. 278 (1882), sub. nom. Condy's Est., 10 W. N. C. 319.

Proceeds of sale of rights to subscribe to insurance company stock allotted to principal. 

Vinton's App., 99 Pa. 434 (1882).

Special cash dividend declared from proceeds of sale of part of corporation's original franchise and property allotted to principal. 

Middleton's App., 103 Pa. 92 (1883).

Gains on a specific sum held for a life tenant belong to residue as against those entitled in remainder to the fund thus bequeathed. 

Phila. Trust, Safe Deposit & Ins. Co.'s App., 24 W. N. C. 

137 (1889), 1 Mona. 230, sub. nom. Turpin's Est., 5 Pa. C. C. 288.

Dividends of profits of a corporation distributed in the form of scrip payable to life tenant. 430

Oliver's Est., 136 Pa. 43 (1890). 

Dividends from a land company over 1,000 per cent on capital caused by discovery of mineral deposits and arising from sale of land allotted to life tenants where capital at time of decedent's death was unimpaired. 

Smith's Est., 140 Pa. 344 (1891); see also 8 Pa. C. C. 323.

Stock dividends declared after decedent's death, representing earnings capitalized in his lifetime allotted to principal. Intrinsic, not market, value at death governs. Prior cases reviewed. 

Thomson's Est., 153 Pa. 332 (1893), 9 Pa. C. C. 639, 28 

W. N. C. 231, 30 W. N. C. 23.

Dividends from an incorporated joint stock company organized to trade in land awarded to income where capital stock as originally invested remained unimpaired. Price realized from sale of rights to subscribe to bonds of another corporation whose stock also was given as a bonus to the subscriber is not income. 

Eisner's Est., 175 Pa. 143 (1896).

Stock bought under rights to subscribe or money realized from sale of such rights belong to principal as does a dividend representing proceeds of a sale by a corporation of a part of its franchise and property. 

Rights to dividend payable in stock of another corporation considered; where rights were issued by corporation A to subscribe to stock of corporation B, the latter were held to be income as a matter of law. (Lease for 999 years by Frankford and Southwark P. R. R. Co. to 

Electric Traction Co.) 

Connolly's Est. (No. 1), 198 Pa. 137 (1901).

Where surplus profits are not declared as income life tenant is not entitled to the enhanced value of stock due to undivided surplus profits. 

Graham's Est., 198 Pa. 216 (1901).

Gains on sale of bonds, the investment of a trustee, inure to principal, as does a dividend representing proceeds of sale of corporation's franchise and property-proceeds of condemnation of part of property of Monongahela Navigation Co. 

Kemble's Est., 201 Pa. 523 (1902).

New shares of stock in another corporation received 10 for 12 for old stock are part of principal but option to subscribe for the stock of the new company is income. (Involves stock of the Metropolitan Traction Company of N. Y. and 

N. J.). 

Robinson's Trust, 218 Pa. 481 (1907).

Dividend obligations issued to shareholders by a corporation (Richmond, F. & P. R. R. Co.) representing a portion of its income applicable to dividends but used by the corporation in the purchase of real estate and permanent improvements allotted to life tenant under the terms of the deed.

APPENDIX 

Boyer's App., 224 Pa. 144 (1909) (a related case).

To the same effect as to the same distributions. Life tenants presumptively entitled to all dividends. Burden on remainderman to show decrease in value fixed at date of execution of deed. 

Stokes's Est. (No. 1), 240 Pa. 277 (1913), 21 Dist. 425.

Profits accumulated prior to death belong to corpus, those subsequent to life tenant whether in cash, scrip or stock. Actual intrinsic value of corpus to be maintained as against result of extraordinary dividend (of L. V. R. R. Co.). 

Stokes's Est. (No. 2), 240 Pa. 288 (1913), 21 Dist. 425.

It is the intrinsic value of assets at death as compared with value at time of declaration of dividends which governs the apportionment. 

Importance of market value as evidence discussed. 

Peterson's Est., 242 Pa. 330 (1913).

Earnings (of Midvale Steel Co.) accumulated and undistributed were "income pure and simple; the fact that they were allowed to accumulate instead of being regularly distributed did not change their character in this regard.'' 

Quay's Est., 253 Pa. 80 (1916).

Profits arising from the sale of stock taken by trustees as part of corpus in lieu of cash was distributable as income under a gift of "income and profits" to the cestui que trust, relying on Stokes' Est. (No. 

1), 240 Pa. 277, supra. 

Wilcox's Est., 66 Super. 182 (1917), 25 Dist. 410.

When the stock of a corporation (the Union Rolling Mills Co.) is by the will of a decedent held in trust by a trustee to pay the income to one person for life, and the principal over to a remainderman, and the corporation at the date of the death of the decedent has a large surplus, so that the book value of the shares is above par, and four years after the death of the life tenant, and after a large addition had been added to the surplus during the life tenancy, the company declares an extraordinary stock dividend equalling practically the amount of the surplus earned since the death of the testator, and at the same time increases its capital stock, selling a large number of the new shares at less than the previous book value of the shares, with the result that all of the shares of the company after the transaction is completed, have a less book value than at the date of the death of the decedent, the stock dividend awarded to the trust estate is not to be distributed wholly to income, but enough of the stock must be set aside to reimburse the principal for the loss it suffered by reason of the stock dividend in connection with the stock increase, but not for any loss due to the sale of new stock at less than the value of the old stock. 

Sloan's Est., 258 Pa. 368 (1917).

When the stock of a corporation (Westinghouse Air Brake Co.) is bequeathed in trust for the use of a beneficiary for life with remainder over, surplus profits accumulated during the testator's life, but not divided until after his death, belong to the corpus of his estate, while

dividends of earnings made after his death, whether in cash, scrip or stock, are income and are payable to the life tenant. 

Thompson's Est., 262 Pa. 278 (1918). 

Stock of a national bank representing profits after the death, distributed to a trustee, belongs to the life tenants. "A trustee has no right to take sides as between the life tenants and remainderman. If he has an election of taking one of several courses, he must take, if possible, that which will not benefit one at the expense of the other.'' 

McKeown's Est., 263 Pa. 78 (1919).

In the distribution of the income of a trust estate, an ordinary corporate dividend is usually payable in its entirety to the party entitled to the income at the time the dividend was declared. 

In the distribution of the income of a trust estate, an extraordinary corporate dividend is presumptively payable to the party entitled to the income at the time the dividend was declared; but this presumption must yield to proof of the fact, and if it appears that by said dividend the corporate assets are reduced below their value at the time the trust began, the principal must first be made good before anything is awarded to income. 

If stock is sold which belongs to the principal of a trust estate, ordinarily all the proceeds belong to the principal. 

If a trust estate holds stock of a corporation which is liquidated, those entitled to the income of the trust are to be awarded so much of the sums received for the stock as they show was income accruing after their rights thereto began, and the balance goes to principal; and this rule is not altered although a sale of the stock is the method pursued in such liquidation.

Veech's Est., 74 Super. 373 (1920). 

The right to subscribe for new shares at par, upon an increase of the capital stock of the corporation (The Standard Oil Co. of N. J.) which is an incident of the ownership of the stock, does not belong as a privilege to the life tenant, but such an increment must be treated as capital and be added to the trust for the benefit of the remainderman. This is equally the rule whether the trustee subscribes for the new stock for the benefit of the trust, or sells the right to subscribe for a valuable consideration. In either event the increase goes to the corpus.

Where a trustee upon the increase of the capital stock of the corporation, sells the right to subscribe to such shares at par, the money derived from such sale goes to the corpus of the estate. 

Waterman's Est., 279 Pa. 491 (1924), rev'g 3 D. & C. 442.

Extraordinary dividend declared by distribution of liberty bonds. 

Held sufficient of these bonds should be awarded to principal as is necessary to make good any reduction in the intrinsic (as distinguished from book) value of the stock, caused by the payment of the dividend. 

Yates's Est., 281 Pa. 178 (1924), af'g 4 D. & C. 569.

Where a trust provides that the income from it shall be paid to one distributee for life, and the principal and remainder to another, ordinarily all the income that accrued during the life estate must be paid

APPENDIX 

to the life tenant, or his personal representative, even though not collected or distributed during his lifetime. 

A life tenant's right to such income, in the absence of very clear language to the contrary, cannot be made to depend on the action or inaction of the trustee. 

Flaccus's Est., 283 Pa. 185 (1925). 

"Increase" construed as synonymous with "income. Extraordinary stock dividends (100%) apportioned to keep intact value of shares as at inception of trust. Rule applicable whether gift of stock be called specific, demonstrative or general. 

Wittmer's Est., 283 Pa. 311 (1925).

Extraordinary stock dividends (of American Natural Gas Co.) ap portioned to maintain intact value, whether they be of cash, scrip or stock. 

Harkness's Est., 283 Pa. 464 (1925), af'g 5 D. & C. 351. 

Same rule applied. 

Mallory's Est., 285 Pa. 186 (1926), rev'g 7 Erie 62, 5 D. & C. 333 (s. c. 5 Erie 277).

Same rule applied. The court considered whole of the surplus existing at the time the dividend (of Ohio Fuel Gas Co.) was declared and not merely so much thereof as was included in the dividend. 

Dickinson's Est., 285 Pa. 449 (1926), rev'g 6 D. & C. 1. 

Intact value must be reduced in case of extraordinary loss (to Fire 

Association of Philadelphia from San Francisco fire) and apportionment of future extraordinary dividends must be based on this new and lower value. Sales of additional stock above par; sales of rights to subscribe and distribution of extraordinary dividend in stock considered and decided according to equitable principles. 

Mandeville's Est., 286 Pa. 368 (1926), afʼg 23 Luz. 347.

Where at the time an account is filed, the value of land companies' stocks left in trust has decreased from the inventory valuation, but extraordinary dividends have been paid from sales of lots, such dividends should be applied to make up the difference between the inventoried value of the stocks and their depreciated value at the time of the filing of the account, and the balance should be distributed as income. 

Nirdlinger's Est., 290 Pa. 457 (1927), mod'g 8 D. & C. 595.

Ordinary dividends belong to life tenants. If distribution of extraordinary dividend, which presumptively belongs to life tenants, impairs intact value it will be apportioned. In case of sale of stock in substance effecting distribution, profit due to an accumulation of income will be apportioned, but income due to "good will" is part of corpus. Life tenant not entitled to accumulated earnings not distributed by corporation as dividends. 

Packer's Est. (No. 1), 291 Pa. 194 (1927). 

Intact value alone governs. Formula for computing and distributing life tenant's share of extraordinary stock dividends.

Jones v. Integrity Trust Co., 292 Pa. 149 (1928), af'g 9

D. & C. 806. 

Intact value alone governs.

Extraordinary stock dividends of United 

Gas Improvement Co. Sales of rights. 

"We now definitely decide that where a corporation gives to the trustees of an estate the right to subscribe for new stock, and they avail themselves of such offer, the benefit resulting therefrom must be apportioned in the same manner as an extraordinary stock dividend would be; that is, there should be allotted to the corpus of the trust sufficient thereof to maintain unimpaired the intact value of the stock held by it, and the life tenant should receive the balance, because it represents corporate earnings which accumulated after he became entitled to all dividends at any time thereafter payable out of such accumulations."' 

Graham's Est., 296 Pa. 436 (1929), afʼg 10 D. & C. 695.

Rights of successive life tenants. Burden of proof and evidence required to overcome presumption that party entitled to income when extraordinary or stock dividend is declared is entitled thereto. 

Buist's Est., 297 Pa. 537 (1929), afʼg 12 D. & C. 159.

Merger and consolidation of corporations considered and defined. 

Life tenant entitled to no part of stock issued par for par in new company. Liberal discretion lodged in trustee binds parties if not abused. 

The life tenant is not entitled to any division until (1) the increased value is declared as a cash dividend, or (2) distributed in the form of a stock dividend, or (3) the affairs of the bank are wound up so that the assets are distributed to those entitled to receive them, or (4) there is a sale of the new stock so that the connection of shareholders is severed. 

Baird's Est., 299 Pa. 39 (1930), afʼg 12 D. & C. 575.

Intact value defined. Fixed as of date of death. Book value the prima facie standard. Proof necessary to overcome this presumption. 

Maris's Est., 301 Pa. 20 (1930), af'g 12 D. & C. 783.

Distribution of proper share of stock dividends to life tenant cannot be thwarted by direction in will that "all stock dividends shall be treated as income' as this is in effect a direction to accumulate income contravening Act of April 18, 1853 (P. L. 503). 

Chauncey's Est., 303 Pa. 441 (1931), af'g 45 Montg. 111.

Burden on remainderman to prove intact value diminished by extraordinary dividends. Profits of corporations from miscellaneous sources. Apportionment considered where surplus partly contributed and partly earned. Effect of merger of corporations. 

Cassatt's Est., 105 Super. 14 (1932).

Gains on sale of stock (of Norfolk & Western Rwy.) representing earnings of the railroad allotted to life tenants though segregated by corporation as "appropriated surplus" account which it used for permanent improvements.

APPENDIX 

Bullitt's Est., 308 Pa. 413 (1932), rev'g 16 D. & C. 376.

Prior adjudication considered as not fixing intact value if not "periodically ascertained and determined.'' Entire record should be examined and facts established. (Virginia Coal and Iron Co.) 

Waterhouse's Est., 308 Pa. 422 (1932), af'g 16 D. & C. 73.

Sets forth complete rules annotated. Outlined in text in full supra, Sec. 243. 

Flinn's Est., 310 Pa. 206 (1932).

In absence of clear and explicit language the intact value of stocks is to be fixed as of the date of the death of the testator (though distributed in this case by executors to trustees five years later). Yearly earnings averaged on a per diem basis where books closed at end of year. 

Opperman's Est. (No. 1), 319 Pa. 455 (1935). 

The unusual circumstances varying the rule that ordinary cash or scrip dividends belong to life tenant must arise from some administrative or corporate act. 

Where dividends from earnings are regularly declared, at uniform intervals, and rates theretofore customarily used, they belong to the life tenants, whether from earnings current or past, and whether or not paid from a surplus account. 

Dividends from earnings since testator's death are payable to the life tenant, without regard to amount or regularity of declaration. 

Where dividends are paid, in whole or in part, out of a fund representing contributed capital, such dividends, regardless of their nature otherwise, must be allocated to the corpus of the trust, to the extent that they are paid from the contributed capital. 

Where an ordinary dividend is received which expresses on its face that it is from contributed capital, or which from prior notice received from the company, the fiduciary should know is from contributed capital, the fiduciary will be held accountable to corpus for the disposition of that dividend.

Where dividends are declared generally, during the lifetime of the testator, though not payable until a later date, they form part of the corpus of the estate, unless such later date is after the death of the testator, in which event they are income. 

Hostetter's Trust, 319 Pa. 572 (1935).

Where the testator of an estate, holding the stock of a corporation which offers its stockholders the right to subscribe to additional stock, exercises such right with funds from the corpus of the estate, the life tenant is, nevertheless, entitled to receive the stock so acquired, without paying into the corpus of the estate the amount of the subscription price, where such stock represents earnings accrued from the time the trust was created to the date of the stock issue, and the intact value of the corpus is maintained unimpaired. 

Flinn's Est., 320 Pa. 15 (1935).

Net earnings derived from a contract held by a corporation at time of testator's death are properly added to capital and surplus in determining the intact value of the stock for purposes of apportioning a stock dividend.

Where testator owned stock of corporation A which later declared a dividend payable in stock of corporation B, the intact value of the latter stock, subsequently sold at a profit, is determined as of the date of its receipt by the trustees and not as of the date of the death of the testator. 

Daily's Est., 323 Pa. 42 (1936), afʼg and mod❜g 24 D. & 

C. 628.

Equitable right of life tenant to ownership of profits cannot be lost by mere inaction of trustee in not dividing shares prior to life tenant's death. Rights of life tenant not defeated by circumstances, or the method of reincorporation adopted. 

Given's Est., 323 Pa. 456 (1936).

Only dividends regularly paid at uniform intervals over a period of years are apportionable under Sec. 22 of the Fiduciaries Act. 

Neafie's Est., 325 Pa. 561 (1937), afʼg 25 D. & C. 608.

Where a trustee in his account allocated the proceeds from the sale of subscription rights to principal, though properly income, and the account so stated was confirmed, as was a subsequent account, without exception thereto by the life tenant, the right of the life tenant to assert that the proceeds from the sale of the subscription rights were income was barred after five years following the confirmation of the first account; nor may it be contended that by reason of the trustees' act in voluntarily writing down the intact value of the shares held in trust, cash to the equivalent of the intact value took the place of the stock as corpus, and that the shares were thus released from any further obligation to the remaindermen and should be treated as income. 

Bullitt's Estate, 308 Pa. 413, distinguished.

Intact value to be preserved for the remaindermen cannot be altered by the trustees, by voluntarily writing the value of the stock up or down, or otherwise, to the prejudice of life tenants or remaindermen. 

A business loss occurring during life tenancy may be charged against surplus or undivided profits accumulated after the death of the testator. 

Ordinarily the court will accept as correct the company's method of charging items when the charges are made in good faith, and the burden of showing bad faith is on the party asserting it. 

In order that there may be distribution to life tenants of earnings accumulated during life tenancy, the corporation must declare a dividend, whether of cash or of stock, the trust estate must receive rights to subscribe, or there must be a liquidation of the corporate assets or of the trust holdings. Where the stock remains in trust unsold, the fact that the corporation has accumulated a surplus from earnings does not entitle the life tenant, in the absence of an abuse of power by the trustee, to the division of such assets of a trust estate, so as to furnish him with these withheld earnings.

The right to surplus undistributed by the corporation whose stock is held in trust does not become fixed in the life, tenant's estate as of the date of his death. Successive life tenants may participate in the distribution of surplus where there is a sale or liquidation of the stock during the life of the trust. 

The remaindermen are entitled to all the value inherent in the stock immediately on the expiration of the life estate in income, except as

APPENDIX 

to ordinary dividends specifically provided for by section 22 of the Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447.

Where there are successive life estates in the income of a trust, and a loss occurs and is charged to surplus, upon sale of the stock, the surplus may be distributed on a proportionate basis each succeeding life tenant bearing his share of the burden of the loss attributable to his undistributed surplus.

The extent to which apportionment may take place between successive life tenants must be governed by the facts in each case, and the conclusion of the court below on such facts will be adopted on appeal unless there is an abuse of power. 

Knox's Est., 328 Pa. 177 (1937).

Outlines rules as to mining stock. Set forth in full in text, supra, Sec. 243, n. 7a. (b) In the lower courts. 

Bishop's Est., 36 Dauph. 17.

The test to be used in the determination of whether property received by a trust estate shall go in whole or in part to the life tenants or to the remaindermen is whether or not payment to the life tenants would cause a diminution in the intact value of the trust estate, that is the value of the trust estate as of the date of its creation. No payments may be made to the life tenants if this value of the trust estate would be impaired. "Income" from corporate stock includes all the earnings for which membership in the company, or ownership of the stock is responsible; but the earning power of the stock is not included. 

Crozer's Est., 26 Del. 328, 27 D. & C. 179.

The legal rights of cumulative preferred stockholders are analogous to those of common stockholders, and dividends on cumulative preferred stock held in trust are, therefore, allocable to income if declared from earnings made subsequent to the creation of the trust, even though the dividends had accrued previously. 

Ormrod's Est., 17 Leh. 82, 28 D. & C. 245.

On the declaration of an extraordinary cash or stock dividend of a corporation (Lehigh Portland Cement Company) during the life tenancy of a trust estate, the rule is to give to the life tenant the income earned since the trust arose, but, at the same time, to preserve intact the corpus as it was at the date of the death of the testator. 

In the modification and change of the capital structure, as to newly issued stock and as to cash, the above stated rule prevails, and, in this case, the entire dividend was awarded to corpus. 

The fact that accrued dividends were due on the preferred stock does not alter the situation. 

Wentz's Est., 45 Montg. 57, 12 D. & C. 398.

A provision in a will creating a trust, to the effect that all stock dividends of proceeds of the sale of rights of subscription to stock shall be treated as principal and not as income, violates section 9 of the Act of April 18, 1853, P. L. 503, forbidding accumulation of in-

come beyond a certain period, and the value of such shares in excess of the amount necessary to maintain the principal at the original value will be awarded to the life tenant. 

Miller's Est., 20 North. 352.

Where the distribution of a stock dividend does not diminish corpus the dividend belongs to the life tenant. 

Corr's Est., 29 Dist. 281 (Phila.).

When a trustee receives shares of stock of a corporation among the assets composing the principal of the trust fund, and the corporation increases its capital by issuing new stock, giving its stockholders the right to subscribe for the new shares at par, if the trustee sells such rights the proceeds of sale belong to the principal of the estate and not to income.

When new stock is issued at par, the actual increase of capital is precisely the amount thus received by the company, and if the new stock has, at the time, an intrinsic value beyond what was paid for it, this presumptively can only be because the holders of the new stock have been put on a footing of equality with holders of old stock, and thus become entitled to share with them in a distribution of assets should the company be dissolved. 

Burton's Est., 12 D. & C. 605, 77 P. L. J. 788 (Phila.).

The proceeds of the sale of rights to subscribe to new stock of a corporation are income as between life tenant and remainderman where such apportionment will not impair the intact value of the stock. 

McCahan's Est., 18 D. & C. 171 (Phila.).

Funds set aside by a corporation out of its earnings as reserves for construction and depreciation, but never used for those purposes nor otherwise applied to capital and remaining unappropriated upon liquidation, are to be treated as income rather than corpus in the distribution of the proceeds of liquidation, as between life tenant and remainderman under a trust owning shares of stock in the corporation. 

A capital gain in the assets of a corporation from the sale of securities, the increase in the value of which does not represent earnings of the issuing corporations, should be awarded to corpus and not to income. 

Miller's Est., 29 Sch. 117.

Where the trustee sells stock and receives a price greater than the value of the stock at the time of the death of the testator, or at the time it was acquired, the profits being due to an accumulation of income, the court should apportion the proceeds between the life tenant and the corpus of the estate, all accumulation of earnings going to the life tenant. 

Stock dividends declared after the death of the testator, above the amount necessary to keep intact the value of the shares as they were at that date, must be distributed as income.

Such rule cannot be set aside even by express provisions in the will that stock dividends shall be considered as principal.

290. PETITIONS. 

Equitable doctrines.32b 

Availability of remedy.33

Essential features.33a 

Recital of parties.34 

In the absence of some impelling reason all petitions should be signed and sworn to by the petitioner.34a 

Right to withdraw a petition.36a

Dismissal of petitioner.seb 

32b See Rules of Practice and Procedure in the Orphans' Courts of Pennsylvania, Section 2, Rules 1 and 2; Sec. 3, Rule 1, Appendix, Vol. II, page 64. 

33 A nonresident may, under Article I, sec. 11, of the Constitution of Pennsylvania, present a petition in a Pennsylvania court. 

The fact that a foreign corporation is not registered to do business in this State under section 1002 of the Business Corporation Law of May 5, 1933, P. L. 

364, does not deprive it of the right to seek relief in Pennsylvania courts if it is not doing any business here. Schoble's Pet 'n, 43 D. & C. 459, af'd in 346 Pa. 318. 

33a See Rules of Practice and Procedure in the Orphans' Courts of Pennsylvania, Section 3, Rule 4, Appendix, Vol. II, page 65. 

Where a petition alleges a breach of an express trust it should set forth, with all the particularity required if it were upon a contract, the terms of the trust and the property to which it relates and, following the practice required in actions of assumpsit brought at law, it should state whether the understanding or trust agreement was oral or written. Gorkiewicz's Est., 43 D. & C. 40. 

34 Particularly where incapacitated. See Rules of Practice and Procedure in the Orphans' Courts of Pennsylvania, Section 3, Rule 3, Appendix, Vol. II, p. 65. 

34a A petition for review of an adjudication is defective under rule 15 (A) of the orphans' court of Philadelphia County if the affidavit thereto is taken by a stranger to the record without any statement as to the authority by virtue of which she acts or her knowledge of the subject, and if the only reason assigned for the failure of the petitioners to execute the petition is that they are both nonresidents, there being no such urgency averred as to prevent the petition being sent to them for execution. Smith's Est., 35 D. & C. 383. 

36a Where the life beneficiary of a trust, who has filed a petition for review of an adjudication of a trustee's account for the purpose of obtaining a termination of the trust and award of principal to him under an alleged power contained in the will, asks leave to withdraw his petition after argument before the court in banc, and his request is opposed by the trustee and other parties in interest who insist that the matter be finally disposed of because petitioner has harassed the trustee over a long period of time and because further proceedings will neces sitate additional counsel fees and costs, the court will refuse to allow him to withdraw the petition, and will dispose of the matter on the merits. Whitaker's 

Est., 35 D. & C. 40. 

36b The orphans' court has authority to dismiss a petition after proper notice and failure of petitioner to appear and argue. McManus' Est., 15 Northumb. 279. [3]

§§ 291, 292 291. ANSWERS. 

Essentials of a proper answer. 38a 

Necessity of an affidavit.38b 

Effect of an answer on the merits.39aa 

38a See Rules of Practice and Procedure in the Orphans' Courts of Pennsylvania, Section 3, Rule 2(a), Appendix, Vol. II, page 64. 

It is not proper practice for a respondent on appeal from probate to incorporate an answer on the merits and an answer raising preliminary objections under Equity Rule 48 and Rule 15 (b) of the orphans' court of Philadelphia County in a single document, and if he does so, so much of the document as is an answer on the merits will be disregarded. Thompson's Est., 35 D. & C. 6. 

38b An answer to a petition to open an audit which has been signed by a trust officer and which had not been affirmed will, nevertheless, be considered by the orphans' court as if the same were in proper form. Donlan's Est., 46 

Lanc. 417. 

39aa The filing of an answer on the merits constitutes a general appearance, despite an attempt in the answer to reserve a jurisdictional question, in the absence of a rule of court authoriizng such a reservation. Schoble Trust Est., 346 Pa. 318, af'g 45 D. & C. 65. 

292. DEMURRERS. 

When appropriate." 40 

Application of equity rules.43a Preliminary objections.44a 

40 A demurrer is a proper plea by which to raise a point of law attacking the legal sufficiency of a prior pleading in the orphans' court. Wagner's Estates, 46 D. & C. 355.

Objections to the jurisdiction of the orphans' court may properly be raised by an answer in the nature of a demurrer, but in such case the facts averred in the petition must be taken as true. Schoble's Pet'n, 43 D. & C. 459, af'd in 346 

Pa. 318. 

43a Where a demurrer discloses that it alleges, inter alia, want of jurisdiction, the court may ignore the demurrer and accept the pleading filed as an answer challenging the jurisdiction of the court. Sullivan's Pet'n, 31 Berks 43, 34

D. &. C. 154. 

44a It is not proper practice for a respondent on appeal from probate to incorporate an answer on the merits and an answer raising preliminary objections under Equity Rule 48 and Rule 15 (b) of the orphans' court of Philadelphia County in a single document and if he does so, so much of the document as is an answer on the merits will be disregarded. 

Equity Rule 55, giving plaintiff a right to file preliminary objections to defendant's answer, means only an answer on the merits: it is neither necessary nor proper to file an answer to preliminary objections, any defenses which might be raised therein being arguable without further pleading. Thompson's Est., 

Preliminary objections to a petition for specific performance of an oral contract to devise realty for want of jurisdiction in the orphans' court and the bar of the statute of frauds were dismissed, with leave to answer to the merits without prejudice to the right to raise the defense of the statute in that pleading. 

The orphans' court has jurisdiction, under section 18, of the fiduciaries act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, to decree specific performance of an oral contract to devise real estate. It is a reenactment of the act of February 24, 1834, P. L. 73. 

Preliminary objection is not the proper procedure to raise the bar of the statute of frauds, where respondents contended that in order to satisfy the statute the testamentary writing should have been executed cotemporaneously with the contract to devise. This defense must be raised by an answer. Kuhn's Est., 89 

P. L. J. 309.

295. REPORTS OF MASTERS AND OTHERS. 

Action of master with respect to exceptions to his report." 

74 Under Rule 8 (h) of the orphans' court of Philadelphia County, it is the duty of a master in an orphans' court proceeding, when exceptions to his report have been filed, to consider each exception seriatim and briefly and concisely to state to the court why he believes each particular exception is not well founded, and if more than one exception relates to the same subject matter or the same proposition of law, such exceptions should be grouped together and may then be answered together; it is not proper practice for the master merely to report that he has considered all of the exceptions and considers none of them well founded. 

Hays' Est., 33 D. & C. 153.

CHAPTER XLVI. 

PROCEDURE TO OBTAIN APPEARANCE. 

297. CITATION AND SERVICE. 

General appearance. 75b Jurisdiction.76 "Any person interested. 99 79 Form and nature of a citation.82 

Procedure not apt, in certain jurisdictions, in the case of tax appeals.84 

Service of the writ.87 

75a The filing of an answer on the merits constitutes a general appearance, despite an attempt in the answer to reserve a jurisdictional question, in the absence of a rule of court authorizing such a reservation. Schoble Trust Est., 346 

Pa. 318, af'g 45 D. & C. 65.

§§ 297, 300 

76 The Court of Common Pleas is without jurisdiction to issue an attachment execution at the suit of a guardian of one minor against another minor's funds received and held by a natural guardian. 

The proper remedy for a creditor seeking to attach a minor's funds in the hands of a guardian is by citation in orphans' court. Lukach v. Salenick, 43 

Lack. 21. 

79 A citation in the orphans' court may issue at the instance of any person interested against a natural guardian who has received funds of a minor. Lukach v. Salenick, 43 Lack. 21. 

82 A citation awarded by the Orphans' Court is a form of process. 

Process is the means of compelling the defendant to appear in court. 

A citation awarded by the Orphans' Court, being a form of process, must issue in the name of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, otherwise the citation is void. 

The petition being the first step in proceedings in the Orphans' Court and the award of a citation the second step, quashing the citation because of fatal defects of form does not warrant setting aside the petition where the petition is in proper form. Gangloff's Est., 8 Sch. Reg. 200, 42 D. & C. 666.

Where a petition for citation to file an account alleges that money was delivered to respondent to be held in trust and charges violation of the terms of the trust based upon part of a letter written by respondent and attached to the petition, petitioner will, upon preliminary objection by respondent, be required to attach a copy of the entire letter as an exhibit, or else aver under oath in his petition that the portion not included is omitted because petitioner has the privilege of refraining from presenting such portion; petitioner will be further required to clarify the averments of his petition so that it can be determined whether or not the relationship between the parties be one of principal and agent, in which case the court would have no jurisdiction. Gorkiewicz's Est., 

84 Section 17 of the Orphans' Court Act of June 7, 1917 (P. L. 363), provid ing, in certain proceedings, for the filing of a petition in the orphans' court and the issuing of a citation, does not prescribe the procedure in an appeal from the appraisement of property of a decedent for inheritance taxation. Schaszberger's Est., 52 York 109, 34 D. & C. 367. 

87 A citation of the orphans' court is the equivalent of an original writ, and service thereof may, under the Orphans' Court Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 363, sec. 17, be made anywhere within the Commonwealth; jurisdiction is thus acquired over a nonresident personally served while within the territorial jurisdiction of the court. Schoble's Pet 'n, 43 D. & C. 459, af'd in 346 Pa. 318.

And see Rules of Practice and Procedure in the Orphans' Courts of Pennsylvania, Section 3, Rule 5 and Section 5, Rules 1-4, Appendix, Vol. II, pages 65-7. 

CHAPTER XLVII. 

PROCEEDINGS TO ENFORCE ORDERS AND DECREES. 

300. METHODS OF PROCEDURE. 

Attachment against garnishee.³ 

Availability of exemption."

Effect of attachment.¹¹ 

3 The procedure on writs of attachment execution issued out of the orphans' court is governed by the Attachment Act of June 16, 1836, P. L. 755, its amendments and supplements, made applicable to such writs by the Act of March 27, 1873, P. L. 49, saved from repeal by the Orphans' Court Act of June 7, 1917,

P. L. 363; and the practice to be followed is that of the common pleas courts, which section 18 (a)4 of the Orphans' Court Act prescribes. Schwartz v. Schwartz 

Where a garnishee is confronted with conflicting claims to a fund in his hands, so that he cannot with safety to himself admit liability to defendant, the court will, upon seasonable application, permit him to pay the money into court and thereby have the court establish which one of the contenders is entitled to the

§§ 300-309 

funds attached, provided that his petition for leave to do so clearly and specifically identifies the claimants and sets forth the nature and character of their alleged claims. Schwartz v. Schwartz, et al., 44 D. & C. 357. 

6 The three-hundred-dollar exemption allowed by the Act of April 9, 1849, P. L. 533, applies only against executions issued on judgments based on contracts express or implied, and is not available against a decree surcharging a fiduciary. 

Schwartz v. Schwartz (No. 1) 42 D. & C. 468.. 

11 Where a trustee was surcharged in a certain amount and thereafter, although specific' reference was made to the amount of the surcharge at four different audits over a period of many years at which he was either present in person or represented by counsel, or of which he had actual notice, he made no objection to the amount and never requested credit for a payment of $3500 to the substituted trustees shortly after the surcharge, and where in addition a writ of attachment was issued against his interest in the estate under section 18 (a) 4 of the Orphans' Court Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 363, on a judgment based on a real debt of the amount of the surcharge with interest, and he took no steps to challenge the attachment or the amount of the judgment, the orphans' court will not, after his death and after the death of other principals in the transaction, allow his estate a credit for the $3,500 payment, especially where it is apparent from the records that he may have been credited with that payment against additional sums for which he may later have become indebted to the estate. Gillespie's Est., 37 D. & C. 375.

CHAPTER XLVIII. 

WITNESSES AND EVIDENCE. 

309. DEPOSITIONS, COMMISSIONS AND LETTERS ROGATORY. 

Discretion of the court as to depositions¹² and as to letters rogatory.

* 

Rules of court.* 

44 43 42 The taking of depositions of witnesses in support of a claim against a decedent's estate is not a matter of right but rests within the sound discretion of the court and leave to take depositions will be granted only upon citation to show cause why it should not be.

The orphans' court will not grant leave to take the testimony of witnesses in support of a claim against a decedent's estate by deposition where it is apparent that the validity of the claim depends largely upon the credibility of the witnesses, since the taking of their testimony by deposition would deprive the court of opportunity to determine their credibility by observing their demeanor or by questioning them, and would deprive the accountant of opportunity for crossexamination. Bolduc's Est., 36 D. & C. 131. 

43 Since a defendant has been compelled to join a legal proceeding, he is prima facie, though not of right, entitled to have his testimony, if a nonresident taken by letters rogatory, but the plaintiff, having brought the proceeding, has no such right: whether a request so to take testimony will be granted is in any event a matter for the discretion of the court. 

The orphans' court will not grant leave to a nonresident claimant to a decedent's estate to take his testimony in a foreign country by letters rogatory merely because he is 85 years of age and infirm, where there are over 24,000 adverse claimants who would be entitled to confront and cross-examine him, where the process would be cumbersome, where the fact that there would be no authority to compel the attendance of witnesses, to compel them to answer, or to punish

$$ 309 them for perjury might prove disadvantageous, and where it would be desirable that the demeanor of the witness be subject to the scrutiny of the court: nor under such circumstances, will leave be given so to take the testimony of other non-official witnesses, especially where it is not alleged that they are likewise aged and infirm. 

The orphans' court, in the exercise of its discretion, will grant leave to have the testimony of officials in a foreign country or their acting representatives taken by deposition in so far as it relates to the proof of formal evidence, which may be questioned only as to the authenticity thereof. Garrett's Est.. 

35 D. & C. 367, af'd in 335 Pa. 287. 

44 See Rules of Practice and Procedure in the Orphans' Courts of Pennsylvania, Section 3, Rule 6, Appendix, Vol. II, page 65. 

311. PRODUCTION OF BOOKS AND PAPERS. 

Applied in the production of an alleged will.47 

47 While the orphans' court is a court of limited jurisdiction, it not only has general equity powers within that jurisdiction, but, without being confined to equity powers and modes of procedure, has generally the right to do whatever is needful to carry out the duties which are within its jurisdiction. "If we may compel discovery of evidence and perpetuate testimony and hold property of a decedent in status quo pending a contest, why may we not take such action as is necessary to preserve the subject-matter of a possible appeal from the register-a testamentary writing? A will is a peculiar instrument in which the tax authorities and creditors and possible legatees and heirs, and in a sense the world generally has an interest, and if special action is required to preserve such writings, this is the place in which to take it. Boni judicis est ampliare jurisdiction. (A maxim meaning: 'It is the duty of a judge to extend his jurisdiction.' See 9 C. J. 135.)" Clunen's Est., 34 D. & C. 490.

The Orphans' Court has jurisdiction of the estate and the fiduciaries from the time of probate and acceptance of the trust by the executors and the mere fact that the information sought for by a petition for inspection of a decedent's papers will later be revealed at the audit of the estate, does not mean that the court cannot hear and grant the petition as a matter of grace. Barbey's Est., 33 

Berks 159, 41 D. & C. 109.

Jurisdiction of a proceeding for an accounting between tenants in common, is primarily in the Court of Common Pleas, but if the question arises in a matter pending in the Orphans' Court, that Court may take jurisdiction. Webb's 

Est., 29 Del. 200. 

57 The orphans' court may properly exercise jurisdiction to determine the ownership of personal property claimed on behalf of a decedent's estate and by the executrix, personally. 

No duty is imposed upon the court to award an issue to the common pleas under section 21 (a) of the Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 363, where no evidence is produced raising a controlling question of fact. Adams' Est., 139 Super. 512. 

The award of an issue to the common pleas to determine whether a decedent executed and delivered an instrument is discretionary and the court is not bound to accept the verdict. Conrad's Est., 333 Pa. 561.

Section 21(a), of the Orphans' Court Act of 1917 (P. L. 393), merely confers upon the orphans' court the power of directing an issue to the court of common pleas to determine a particular question of fact as to which the judge of the orphans' court is in doubt; but the exercise of this power is discretionary with the court, and the court is not bound to send such an issue to the jury unless it is deemed essential to a proper disposition of the case. 

Where the terms of an oral contract were not in dispute, but the controversy arose from the interpretation thereof, the court refused to send the matter to the common pleas for trial before a jury. Walker's Est., 53 York 1.

Where there is a substantial dispute as to a fact or facts upon which the question of the jurisdiction of the orphans' court depends, it must award an issue, but where the facts are not in dispute the question becomes one solely of law to be decided in limine. Welch's Est., 32 D. & C. 231. 

58 The orphans' court must, under certain circumstances, award an issue devisavit vel non upon request where there is a substantial dispute as to the validity of a will, but it may also, under Section 21(a) of the Orphans' Court Act of June 7, 1917 (P. L. 363), as amended by the Act of July 1, 1937 (P. L. 

2665), send any issue of fact to a jury of its own volition.

Even though proponents produce no evidence in support of a will, a hearing judge may properly award an issue devisavit vel non where the contestant's evidence in support of her allegation that the will was forged consists of an alleged confession, as to which there are many uncertain elements that may well go to the credibility of the witness, and opinion evidence. Livezey's Est., 31 

D. & C. 459. (See also Secs. 29, 30 and 31 supra.)

The Orphans' Court has power to send an issue to the Court of Common Pleas for the trial of facts by a jury whenever they shall deem it expedient so to do;

§§ 314, 317 

and where the auditor of the estate of a decedent is of opinion that an issue should be framed, and files with his report a request for an issue, and where the question is the genuineness of a signature to a note, and where there were a large number of witnesses on both sides of the question, the Court awarded a precept to the question of fact before a jury. Knight's Est., 5 Northumb. 160.

Where there is a substantial factual dispute as to ownership, the orphans' court has no power, sitting as a fact-finding tribunal, to try and determine this question, but may submit the issue for a trial by jury, and a verdict so found will properly constitute the basis of a decree by the orphans' court settling the controversy.

If the proofs show that the denial of the plaintiff's right is not based upon facts which in law show a substantial dispute, so that if the case were before a jury binding instructions against the defendant would be justified, then the court may administer the relief asked, and it is not necessary that the right of the plaintiff should be first settled at law, or that an issue should be granted to determine the question of the title set up by the defendant. Brown's Est., 343 Pa. 230. 

Title being prima facie in the estate, it was exclusively for the orphans' court to determine, in limine, whether the evidence disclosed a substantial dispute as to ownership of the asset, and the court of common pleas was without jurisdiction to entertain the cause until and unless the orphans' court, having first determined that question in plaintiff's favor, should have submitted to it for trial the issue of title. Landis v. Landis, 343 Pa. 252. 

59 Where there is a substantial dispute as to the ownership of property in the possession of decedent at time of death, the orphans' court has no power to try and determine this question, but may, under the Act of June 7, 1917 (P. L. 363), Section 21(a), submit the issue to the court of common pleas for a trial by jury.

The issue of decedent's ownership of property may be tried in the common pleas upon the precept of the orphans' court defining the precise question in dispute, without further pleadings. 

The determination of an issue in the common pleas, as certified to the common pleas by the orphans' court, involving a jurisdictional fact, is conclusive on the orphan's court. Keyser's Est., 329 Pa. 514.

Where there is a substantial, factual dispute as to ownership, the orphans' court has no power, sitting as a fact-finding tribunal, to try and determine this question, but may submit the issue for a trial by jury, and a verdict so found will properly constitute the basis of a decree by the orphans' court settling the controversy.

Where a person claims ownership of property known to be in testator's possession at his death, the orphans' court has jurisdiction to determine whether a substantial dispute exists as to the ownership of the property. 

If at testator's death the property is shown to have been in his possession, or if for any other reason it was presumably his, a mere denial of his ownership unsupported will not oust the orphans' court of its jurisdiction, but the court may proceed with the investigation so far as to inform itself whether the denial is made in good faith and a substantial dispute exists. Crisswell's Est., 334 Pa. 

266, af'g 86 P. L. J. 615, 52 York 165.
